Australian tennis player Nick Kyrgios provisionally suspended after failing cocaine test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:51:21 UTC
19:51:21 KST

Dilara Hamit
19 August 2026•Update: 19 August 2026
Australian tennis player Nick Kyrgios has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for a bodily remnant of cocaine, the International Tennis Integrity Agency (ITIA) announced Wednesday.
Kyrgios, 31, provided a sample during an ATP 250 tournament in Mallorca, Spain, on June 22, according to an ITIA statement.
A World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA)-accredited laboratory confirmed on July 17 that the sample contained benzoylecgonine, a metabolite of cocaine, meaning a molecule resulting from cocaine being metabolized by the body.
Cocaine is classified as a stimulant and substance of abuse on WADA’s Prohibited List and is banned during competition under the Tennis Anti-Doping Program. Reduced sanctions can apply when its use is determined to have occurred outside competition.
The ITIA said a provisional suspension was mandatory because of the nature of the substance and had been in effect since Aug. 4.
Kyrgios has the right to appeal the suspension but had not done so as of Wednesday, the agency added.
While suspended, he is prohibited from playing, coaching at or attending events organized or sanctioned by the ATP, WTA, Grand Slam tournaments, World Tennis, or national tennis associations.
“I recently failed a drug test in Mallorca after testing positive for cocaine. I made a huge mistake and I take full responsibility for it,” Kyrgios said in a statement posted on US social media platform Instagram.
He apologized to his fans, family, sponsors, and young people who follow him, saying he was “deeply disappointed” in himself.
Kyrgios said years of injuries had taken a physical and mental toll and that coming to terms with nearing the end of his career had been difficult, though he stressed that this did not excuse his actions.
He described the positive test as a “wake-up call” and said he would step away from social media and public life for 28 days to focus on his recovery.
Kyrgios reached a career-high singles ranking of world No. 13 in October 2016 and advanced to the Wimbledon final in 2022, where he lost to Novak Djokovic.
Injuries to his knee and wrist have severely restricted his appearances in recent seasons. He played only four singles matches this year and most recently competed in the Wimbledon men’s doubles event alongside Alexander Bublik, with the pair losing in the opening round.

====================================================================================================

the nakagin capsule tower and the dream of a home that could change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:50:49 UTC
19:50:49 KST

kisho kurokawa’s plug-in home
In Tokyo’s Ginza district, Kisho Kurokawa’s Nakagin Capsule Tower once looked less like a conventional apartment building than a piece of infrastructure waiting for its next component. Completed in 1972, the project stacked 140 prefabricated capsules around two reinforced-concrete cores, proposing a radically different idea of what a home could be: a replaceable part of a larger organism. It was one of the clearest built expressions of Japanese Metabolism, the postwar architectural movement that imagined buildings and cities as systems capable of growth and transformation (read more here).
The main concept was deceptively simple. The concrete cores were intended to remain, while the capsules attached to them could eventually be removed and replaced. Kurokawa imagined the building behaving like a living system, with its individual parts changing as technology, habits, and the needs of its inhabitants changed. The apartment was no longer necessarily something designed once and then preserved, but it could be upgraded and adapt to the evolving needs of its inhabitants. That distinction matters, as much of twentieth-century housing is based on permanence. Buildings are completed, sold, occupied, maintained, and eventually demolished.
Kisho Kurokawa, Architect & Associates (Tokyo, est. 1962). Nakagin Capsule Tower, Tokyo. 1970–72. exterior view. 1972 | image by Tomio Ohashi
the home as a replaceable component
Nakagin’s architecture anticipated its own obsolescence. The idea belonged to a particular moment in Japan. The Metabolists emerged in the years of rapid postwar reconstruction and economic growth, when the scale and speed of change in Japanese cities made conventional architectural permanence seem increasingly inadequate. Kurokawa, alongside figures including Kiyonori Kikutake and Fumihiko Maki, imagined architecture as something closer to biology than classical composition. Cities could grow, buildings could regenerate, components could come and go. Nakagin gave that proposition a physical form.
The two cores of the tower rise 11 and 13 stories, carrying circulation and the primary services of the building. Around them, the capsules project outward in an irregular arrangement, producing the characteristic clustered facade. Each module measures roughly 2.5 by 2.5 by 4 meters and contains about 10 square meters of space. Manufactured away from the construction site and brought to Tokyo largely complete, the capsules belong as much to the language of industrial production as they do to architecture. Inside, the logic becomes even clearer.
The compact rooms are fitted with molded bathroom units, storage, desks, beds, and built-in electronics. A television, radio, tape deck, digital clock, and desk calculator turn the capsule into a machine for living. A circular window at the end of each unit makes the occupant feel like they have entered a piece of equipment rather than a conventional apartment. This was habitation designed around mobility, around an intended resident, the urban salaryman, someone who could spend the working week in the center of Tokyo without requiring the domestic infrastructure of a conventional home. Dining, laundry, entertainment, and social life could happen elsewhere. The capsule provided the private minimum necessary for life inside an enormous city.
Kishō Kurokawa in front of the completed Nakagin Capsule Tower, 1974. image by Tomio Ohashi
The capsule was meant to be temporary
The most radical part of Nakagin was the assumption that its individual rooms would not last forever. Kurokawa’s system separated the building into two kinds of time. The cores were conceived as long-lived infrastructure. The capsules were shorter-lived equipment, expected to be replaced roughly every 25 to 35 years. In theory, a worn or obsolete capsule could be unbolted from the structure and exchanged for a new one while the larger building continued to operate.
This distinction between frame and infill is central to the Metabolist imagination. A building could have a permanent skeleton without having permanent rooms. Architecture could accommodate change without starting again from zero. There is something almost ordinary about the proposition today. We are accustomed to upgrading phones, computers, cars, appliances, and other components of everyday life. Kurokawa was extending that logic to architecture. The capsule was a piece of industrial technology attached to a larger spatial network. The concept also carried a distinctly Japanese understanding of impermanence. Kurokawa connected his architecture to mono no aware, the awareness of transience and the emotional recognition that things change and disappear. His idea of ‘cyborg architecture’ suggested an architecture in which people, machines, infrastructure, and buildings existed in continuous exchange. But a theory of change is not the same thing as a mechanism for change. The history of Nakagin is the story of what happens when those two things diverge.
facade of the iconic building in Tokyo | image by Noritaka Minami
when a flexible building becomes difficult to alter
For all its apparent modularity, the tower proved remarkably difficult to metabolize. The capsules were attached independently to the cores, and their connections were conceived to allow removal. Yet the physical arrangement of the building introduced a problem that became increasingly consequential with age. The modules were installed in sequence, with tightly constrained gaps between them. Removing a capsule from lower or middle levels was not as simple as disconnecting four bolts and lifting it away. Access to one unit could depend on the capsules positioned above it. The building that appeared to consist of discrete parts was, in practice, deeply interdependent.
Modularity is often presented as a synonym for flexibility, but a collection of modules is not automatically an adaptable system. The connections between those modules matter. So does the sequence of assembly, access for maintenance, replacement logistics, and the infrastructure running between them. A capsule could be conceptually independent while remaining physically embedded in everything around it.
There was another problem, perhaps even more fundamental: the building did not belong to one person. Over time, the units acquired different uses and different values for their occupants. Some became residences, while others were used as offices, studios, hobby rooms, or storage. The original demographic imagined by Kurokawa also changed as the city changed, a fragmentation that made large-scale renewal difficult. Replacing capsules was a collective financial and legal decision, one that involved owners with different priorities and different capacities to pay. The metabolism of the building had become a matter of governance, and governance is rarely as fluid as architectural concepts and drawings.
Noritaka Minami. B1004 I, from the series 1972 (2010–22). 2011. archival pigment print, 20 × 25″ (101.6 × 127 cm) image © Noritaka Minami
fifty years of habitation changes the meaning of a room
There is a temptation to look at Nakagin only through the eyes of its architect, to see it as a futuristic object that failed to become the future, but the lives lived inside the capsules complicate that interpretation. The rooms were designed for a very particular mode of urban existence. They took for granted that the resident would remain highly connected to the city beyond the apartment. The capsule could be private without being self-sufficient. It was a place to sleep, work, store things, and retreat briefly before returning to the metropolis.
Over five decades, however, the city around it changed, and so did the meaning of the capsules. The same ten-square-meter rooms could become studios, storage spaces, personal retreats, or low-cost places to work. Their smallness, initially presented as a technologically enabled lifestyle, acquired other meanings. A space designed as an efficient corporate pied-à-terre could become valuable precisely because it offered something different from the lifestyle originally intended. People did not inhabit the architecture according to the script written for them, they also had the option to adapt it.
By the time Nakagin entered its final decades, the gap between its futuristic image and its physical condition had become difficult to ignore. The construction of the tower relied on industrially produced steel and concrete components, but its systems still had to endure the ordinary pressures of weather, moisture, plumbing, mechanical failure, maintenance, and age. Exterior panels deteriorated, pipes corroded, leaks persisted, hot-water systems failed, and individual air-conditioning units reached the end of their lives. The building also contained asbestos insulation installed to meet fire-safety requirements at the time of construction. As deterioration increased, the presence of hazardous material became another obstacle to intervention. Repair was no longer a question of replacing a component. It could involve remediation, specialist work, and costs that made the idea of routinely exchanging capsules increasingly remote.
There was also the matter of land. Nakagin occupied a valuable site in Ginza, one of Tokyo’s most intensely developed districts. As land values and expectations for urban density changed, the relatively low-density tower became increasingly difficult to justify economically. The unusual organization of the building, so important to its identity, also limited how efficiently the site could be used.
image courtesy of Nakagin Capsule Tower Building Preservation / Regeneration project
a building that became more valuable after it disappeared
The struggle over Nakagin’s future continued for years. Preservationists, architects, and heritage organizations argued that the building represented an important surviving work of Metabolism and a rare opportunity to preserve the ideas of the movement in built form. Kurokawa himself proposed replacing the old capsules with new ones and restart the cycle that had never taken place. But the technical, financial, and organizational obstacles proved too great. The tower began to come down in 2022. Its demolition might have been the final contradiction: a building designed to replace its parts ended up losing its entire body. Twenty-three capsules were salvaged during the dismantling process. They were carefully removed, treated for hazardous materials, restored, and dispersed to institutions and other settings. The capsule, finally, became mobile.
One of the best-known surviving units, Capsule A1305, entered the collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Other capsules moved into museums, cultural institutions, and new uses in Japan. Some have been adapted as spaces for accommodation or display. Their new lives are different from the ones Kurokawa imagined. They are no longer interchangeable pieces in a constantly evolving residential machine. They are fragments of a vanished building.
Nakagin Capsule Tower Building, Ginza White Ark | image courtesy of the Museum of Modern Art, Saitama
what nakagin teaches us about adaptable housing
One way to read Nakagin Capsule Tower is as a failed utopia, but failure is not necessarily the most useful conclusion. Nakagin remains compelling because it exposes a problem that contemporary architecture is still trying to solve. Modular construction, prefabricated housing, micro-apartments, circular building systems, and design for disassembly all promise buildings that can respond to changing circumstances. The language has changed, but the underlying question is still, how can architecture accommodate lives that do not stay still?
Kurokawa answered by separating the building into parts. The experience of Nakagin suggests that the answer has to go further. A genuinely adaptable home needs adaptable ownership, accessible infrastructure and repairable materials, regulations that permit change. It needs a financial model capable of supporting replacement. And perhaps most importantly, it needs to recognize that inhabitants will keep reinterpreting the spaces they are given. The capsule was a proposition about how people might live, a proposition that changed once people actually lived there.
night time at the Nakagin Capsule Tower, with Mr. Takayuki Sekine seen through the window of capsule B1004, 2016. image © Jeremie Souteyrat
There is a particular poignancy to seeing photographs of Nakagin today. The circular windows, clustered capsules, and weathered panels look like a fragment of a future that arrived early and then did not behave as predicted. But perhaps that is why the building belongs in a conversation about habitation now. Its greatest lesson is that habitation is too complicated to be solved by modularity alone. A home is entangled with ownership, infrastructure, maintenance, labor, economics, regulation, technology, memory, and the changing habits of the people who occupy it.
Kisho Kurokawa imagined the capsule as a cell in an urban organism, which he wanted to be replaceable so that the organism could continue living. The organism aged around its cells until the entire structure became unsustainable. And yet, after demolition, the cells began to move. Perhaps that is the strange afterlife of Nakagin: the building could not achieve impermanence while it was alive, but its fragments became impermanent once it was gone. The capsules traveled, entered collections, became exhibitions, reconstructed interiors, digital models, and objects of study. For a movement that imagined the city as something closer to a living organism, it is an appropriately complicated ending. Nakagin does not survive as its predicted. It’s still alive as evidence of how difficult it is to build a future that remains open.

The tribal residents have been holding a Satyagraha against the project, demanding adequate compensation and dignified rehabilitation for people whose land is being acquired.
NEW DELHI: Congress leader and leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, on Wednesday backed tribal residents of Madhya Pradesh’s Bundelkhand region protesting against the Ken-Betwa River Link Project, saying the Congress stands with them and promising to visit the protest site to pressure the government over their demands for compensation and rehabilitation.Rahul shared a video on X featuring accounts from tribal residents affected by the project and said, "The problems, demands, struggles, and personal ordeals of the tribal brothers and sisters who are carrying out a satyagraha against the Ken-Betwa project--their own account. For years, these residents of Bundelkhand have been enduring injustice and oppression solely for their rights; they deserve respect and support," he said."In this fight of our tribal brothers and sisters, I and the Congress stand with them," he said.In the video, a tribal representative claimed that the project would affect 21 tribal-dominated villages and lead to the loss of around 4.6 million trees, besides affecting the Panna Tiger Reserve. The representative also claimed that around 11,500 acres of land belonging to nearly 7,000 families would be affected.
The residents urged Rahul to raise their concerns about alleged administrative harassment in Parliament and join their movement.
Rahul assured them that he would visit the site and put pressure on the government.The tribal residents have been holding a Satyagraha against the project, demanding adequate compensation and dignified rehabilitation for people whose land is being acquired.Rahul had also supported the agitation earlier in July. Sharing a poem and visuals from the protest, he said the tribal residents were demanding fair compensation through non-violent means and described tribal people as the "original owners of the country"."The tribal brothers and sisters of Madhya Pradesh had sat on a water satyagraha and hunger strike because their land was taken away for the Ken-Betwa project, but they received neither fair compensation nor dignified rehabilitation. The 'truth' is that tribals are the original owners of the country--the first right to water, forests, and land belongs to them alone. And their 'satyagraha' is because that very right is being snatched from them today.""In their unique way, their demand is simply this: provide a proper means of livelihood--or else life is no different from a funeral pyre. But even this is unacceptable to the BJP government. Instead of listening to them, their peaceful protest is being crushed with police force. We stand with our tribal brothers and sisters. We will secure justice for them--compensation and rehabilitation will have to be provided," he added.The Ken-Betwa Link Project is a major river-linking initiative aimed at transferring surplus water from the Ken river in Madhya Pradesh to the Betwa river through a 221-km-long link canal. The project is being implemented in the drought-prone Bundelkhand region of Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
The Rs 44,605-crore project is the first river-linking project under the National Perspective Plan. According to the government, it is expected to irrigate 1.062 million hectares, provide drinking water to around 6.2 million people and generate hydropower.The project involves construction of the 77-metre-high Daudhan Dam and two tunnels in the Ken river basin in Panna. The government says the project will enable irrigation across 8.11 lakh hectares in 2,000 villages across 10 districts and benefit around seven lakh farmer families.It is also expected to provide drinking water to 44 lakh people in Madhya Pradesh and 21 lakh people in Uttar Pradesh, while generating 103 MW of hydropower and 27 MW of solar energy.

The Swiss government has announced a CHF800 million budget surplus for 2026, having initially forecast a large deficit.
The revised figures come after parliament approved an austerity plan to prevent losses in the coming years.
The government had forecast a deficit of CHF700 million for 2026, but the sharp rise in corporation tax revenue has improved the financial outlook, it said in a statement.

Additional revenue is also expected from Geneva. The Federal Council’s upward revisions take into account an additional CHF970 million credit for the armed forces in the 2026 budget.
They are also being taken into account for the 2027 budget and the austerity plan adopted this year, the government says.

We Bought a $500 Counterfeit Rolex So Good, Even Rolex Didn’t Spot It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

“Would you like a glass of champagne?” Even though I'm painfully thirsty and nervous beyond belief, I decline the salesperson's offer.
I’m sitting upstairs in Rolex’s flagship London store on Old Bond Street. I’ve just handed over a fake Rolex to the staff and requested that its bracelet be adjusted, a simple bit of maintenance that requires removing a few links. I haven’t volunteered that the watch is a phony, but I haven’t said it’s legit, either.
My imposter Oyster Perpetual is now on a workbench in the glass-fronted servicing room on the second floor. I can see staff in white lab coats working diligently as a salesperson joins them to carefully examine the timepiece before downsizing the metal bracelet.
This replica is one of a few WIRED has purchased on the internet. So far, nobody in the store has spotted that the watch is a fake. Surely the game's about to be up? Maybe there’s just time to slip away before the police are called.
After what feels like far too long, the salesperson returns. He, like his colleagues downstairs did when I arrived, congratulates me on a beautiful watch and hands me back the counterfeit timepiece, now perfectly sized. The removed links have been placed reverently in a delicate, tiny paper bag, marked with the Rolex logo in cadmium green. Heart still pounding, I walk out.
Purchasing a counterfeit Swiss watch used to mean haggling at a Canal Street market stall or ducking into a Hong Kong back alley, where an approximation of a Rolex, Patek Philippe, or Audemars Piguet could be picked up for $50. If it survived beyond the flight home, that felt like a bonus. Now, though, the era of the “super clone” has arrived.
Mass-produced in huge quantities by Chinese factories, these watches are sold through dealers who advertise on TikTok and Instagram, broker through WhatsApp, and arrange discreet delivery to your door. Since reputation by word-of-mouth is paramount (these businesses can’t exactly show their wares in a digital shop window), they even claim to offer customer service channels, warranties, repair centers, and guarantees to send a replacement if your purchase is seized by customs.
In dedicated forums on Reddit and other websites, strictly moderated communities spread gossip about factories being raided by authorities, offer sketchy legal advice, upvote buyers’ photos of fake Rolexes worn behind the wheels of Lamborghinis, and even offer quality control services.
Quality control, or QC, is at the heart of this community. The subreddit r/RepTime has 269,000 weekly visitors and over 18,000 weekly contributions, according to Reddit’s own statistics. Posts about new counterfeit watch purchases pile up by the hour, both in r/RepTime and r/RepTimeQC, the offshoot subreddit focused on quality control. The posts contain photographs sent from the dealer to the customer, who then seeks advice from the RepTime community on whether they should “GL” (green-light) or “RL” (red-light) their purchase.
Every post must follow a strict format, demonstrating that the buyer has put effort into understanding the QC process and assessing their own watch before seeking the approval of the community and its moderators. As with other high-traffic subreddits, new accounts cannot post right away and instead must earn comment karma by communicating in other, more open subreddits first. Without that, posts are automatically intercepted and deleted before they appear in public and pollute the feed.
The posts are stuffed with coded language. Beyond the usual watch-world reference numbers and model nicknames (like a 124060 Sub, or a “Hulk” and “Pepsi”), there are factory names, often abbreviated to two or three letters, and aliases of every TD, or “trusted dealer.”
There’s earnest talk of gaps around the SELs (solid end links of a bracelet), the shortening of “genuine” and “replica” to “Gen” and “Rep,” and an aesthetic grading system for the cloned watches going from “1:1,” “Super Rep,” and the best of the best, “NWBIG,” which stands for “Not Worth Buying in Gen”—replicas considered so accurate that buying the genuine article is deemed entirely unnecessary.
The insidery shop talk might appeal to the devotees, but it doesn't exactly disguise what's going on—not that some community members seem to care about the potential illegality of replica timepieces. Numerous claims of shipments being intercepted and seized are batted away with advice to ignore letters received from customs.
Despite hundreds of quality-control requests landing in the subreddit every month, one source tells us that 98 percent of them are picked up by just three moderators. “Helping people with our comments is what we truly enjoy, and it’s the reason we spend so much time on the sub,” says one moderator, who asked to remain anonymous due to their fear of legal repercussions. They add that one of the group’s moderators “is a professional watchmaker,” but that others are amateurs in the field.
Are they concerned about the ethical implications of what they are doing? “I’m in the USA, and it is not illegal to buy or own replica watches,” the moderator says. “It is illegal to sell a replica and claim it is genuine. I am very strongly opposed to that. In fact, on the rare occasion that someone mentions more than a passing interest in a replica watch I am wearing, I volunteer that the watch is a replica.”
Even a Reddit community with more than a quarter of a million weekly visitors represents a mere fraction of the global fake-watch industry. The Federation of the Swiss Watch Agency has estimated that tens of millions of fake watches are produced every year, dwarfing the number legitimately manufactured by Swiss brands. And, while many super clones sell for between $500 and $700, there are cases of ultra counterfeits posing as watches worth millions.
“There’s a very well-known Patek,” says counterfeit watch expert Adrian Hailwood, referring to an automatic model with the reference number 3448. It was the first serially produced automatic perpetual calendar wristwatch, and there have long been rumors that two examples were made in rose gold for a South American retailer. Only one is publicly known, a 1968 example first sold in Uruguay. In 2011 it was sold at auction by Christie’s for CHF 2,099,000 (about $2.3 million at the time), then sold again in 2025 for CHF 2.7 million (about $3.3 million).
“Allegedly there’s another one,” Hailwood says. “But I’ve seen three—all pretending to be that one, and all of them with faults. So somebody is churning out rose gold 3448s. And if it’s potentially got a list price of a million pounds, there’s a lot of incentive to put them together.”
Hailwood says that because such a piece would have real Patek innards and a totally fake outside, requiring a lot of work and resources and access to parts, each would cost between £20,000 to £30,000 to create. “You can imagine someone going, ‘Look, we can’t put this through public auction, it would be a million pounds. But, say, £400,000 and ask me no more questions.’ People with more money than sense would potentially go for that,” he says.
Million-dollar Pateks tend not to crop up on r/RepTime. Instead, the vast majority of watches subjected to quality control checks are replica Rolexes. Posts scrutinizing the fine details of Submariners, Datejusts, and Daytonas are especially frequent, along with a smattering of Tudor, Omega, IWC, and Cartier replicas. Most tend to be stainless steel, since their low manufacturing cost means these clone watches cannot be made from real precious metal.
QC photos are taken after a watch has been produced and paid for, usually with cryptocurrency sent from buyer to dealer. The aim of the QC photo is to show the dial from dead center, which helps the customer check for common faults such as misaligned hour markers. This is done by drawing lines on the images between markers to check that they are level, or by using an online tool that has premade ruler templates for the most popular Rolexes.
Helpfully, QC posts include the names of the dealer and factory, the model of watch, and a set of checks for index alignment, dial printing, date wheel alignment if applicable, hand alignment, and bezel. They often include data on the watch’s movement, shown in a dealer-produced video of the piece being tested on a timing device known as a timegrapher. Dealer contact details and links to websites advertising counterfeit products are not shared—and Reddit has removed some content for violating its trademark policy—but it only takes a couple of clicks to find exhaustive purchasing guides elsewhere.
As long as the poster has done their homework and provided a thorough assessment of the watch, a moderator will respond with feedback like: “You did a pretty good job with the QC tool. Index aligns superbly and the bars are straight. Bezel engraving is solid and dial printing strong. Bezel pip looks centered and SELs are good with maybe the bottom right one showing its pin in one pic … [timegrapher] numbers are within range. If you’re ready to GL, GL and wait for the magic box to arrive. Enjoy.” Some responses are more blunt: “All good, but you knew that. GL.”
Amazingly, the aesthetic standard of these super clone replicas is so high that almost every QC’d watch gets a green light. In the rare event of a red light—one mod estimates that RLs are recommended only 5 percent of the time—the buyer asks the seller for another replica, which is often offered up without much protest.
Buying Time
To test for ourselves just how easy buying super clones actually is, WIRED followed the online advice of the Reddit communities to buy three different clone Rolexes of our own from a dealer called “JTime.”
We chose two classics, a replica Submariner for $438 and a Daytona at $768—plus, in an attempt to throw a wrench in the gears, one potentially harder to duplicate accurately, an Oyster Perpetual “Celebration” with its intricate multicolored bubble dial for $498.
The Sub and Daytona were classified on the community’s master spreadsheet as being NWBIG. The Celebration was listed a step below at “VG,” or very good. We had to contact JTime through WhatsApp and pay using the stablecoin USDT (though some dealers, including ours, take credit card payments if you’re feeling particularly foolish). Two of our watches would be ordered from one factory called Clean, with the Celebration model from another called VSF. Both are in China.
A few days after sending JTime a screenshot of the successful crypto transfer, email photos came through showing our watches. All three looked immaculate, even the Celebration model. After earning enough Reddit karma to post (which took some time, meaning we had to stall our dealer), we dropped the dealer images on RepTime’s QC channel for evaluation, hoping to get a thumbs-up from the apparent king of quality assessors, “WatchYoda,” whose opinion seems to carry considerably more weight than any other.
Sadly, perhaps feeling a disturbance in the force, WatchYoda didn't engage on our posts, but other assessors gave our pieces the GL.
Within weeks, cardboard boxes arrived with shipping labels claiming the contents to be men’s polyester pants worth $15. All three watches were protected by plastic wrapping and rubber bezel guards bearing the factory name. The Celebration even came with an obviously fake Rolex warranty card.
All three arrived as aesthetically described by JTime, looking remarkably genuine, even down to micro-adjustment mechanisms in their bracelets, and all kept accurate time.
However, one vital detail slipped through the super-clone QC process unchecked: We ordered a 36-mm Oyster Perpetual Celebration, but what arrived was a 41 mm. To those not familiar with the watch world, this may seem inconsequential, but to watch buyers this equates to being sent, at best, a suit that doesn’t fit, and at worst an entirely different outfit.
This grave error wasn’t remedied with the offer of a refund or a swap for the correct size, but instead the proposal of a small discount on a future purchase. It’s still very much “buyer beware” in the world of super clones.
Still, the entire process, from crypto payment to QC evaluation on Reddit to the shipper-tracked watches arriving, had taken less than a month. For the princely sum of $1,704, we had not one, but three utterly convincing replica Rolexes, even if one was completely the wrong size.
For a thorough expert evaluation of our cloned watches, WIRED met Adrian Hailwood at the UK offices of Watch Collecting, an online watch auction platform he helped launch in 2021, and for which he now provides authentication services. Since much of the production cost of super clones goes on the dial, Hailwood suggested inspecting other parts of the watch.
Under the jeweler’s loupe, he spotted bracelet screws that “really aren’t very round,” and the underside of a clasp that “is very much raw metal” and “not particularly nice.” These imperfections were followed by a Rolex logo on the bracelet which had been “milled out quite amateurishly … Almost looks like someone has done it with a Dremel.”
Hailwood plowed on. “The luminous material looks like it’s not set particularly nicely … The pip is not centered in the triangle, and it’s slightly too yellow for a modern watch.”
One startling piece of accuracy, however, is the coronet (Rolex’s crown-like logo), which since the early 2000s has been laser-etched discreetly into the 6 o’clock position of the sapphire crystal. A couple of millimeters wide and only visible under bright light, the supposed anti-counterfeit measure was present in our replica Submariner. On some fakes the coronet is fudged with a sticker or crudely scratched into the back of the sapphire. Other times it seems genuine, but fails to match the original, which is made up of tiny stars of varying sizes, not just the etched dots of the counterfeit.
Opening the watch revealed a replica movement that looked, at first glance, very much like the real deal. It appeared to be “reasonably good,” but then Hailwood pointed out how there’s a balance regulating arm to help fine-tune how quickly the watch runs—a type of movement that Rolex hasn’t used since 1957. Rolex now uses movements with free-sprung balances, so, in a bid to fool authenticators, counterfeiters have been known to swap the whole assembly around, obscuring the balance components. “That caught a lot of people out,” Hailwood says.
Since WIRED’s watches were examined, however, the counterfeiters have already upped their game. Hailwood claims free-sprung balances have now been introduced across clone movements imitating those by Rolex, Patek Philippe, Richard Mille, and Audemars Piguet. Once a relatively small-volume upgrade, these are now “industrialized features” that eliminate one of the tells he identified in our replica Submariner.
“The investment to produce this kind of clone movement … this is not back-alley sweatshop stuff,” says Hailwood, “this is big factories investing millions to produce full-on clones. It’s said by some watchmakers that these are now close enough that they can be serviced with Rolex parts, which does raise the specter of someone taking a genuine Rolex balance out and swapping it in [to a fake].”
Can there ever be justification for owning a replica watch? The community claims so. Most commonly it’s a love of the design backed up by a simple “because I can.” Some profess to own the real thing and simply want to see how closely they can match it with a fake.
Others suggest they’re a good option for people in watch-crime hot spots such as London or Milan, where it’s too dangerous to wear the real deal out in the open. The preferred approach is to lock the genuine article in a safe at home and strap a replica to your wrist when out in public. In this manner, the super clone morphs into some form of luxury decoy or insurance policy.
This works in the art world, where billionaires are urged not to display real Monets on yachts, and among the very highest echelons of classic car collecting, where insurers would rather you don’t take your $50 million Ferrari on the racetrack. In both cases, an exact replica can be a sensible solution.
Of course, it’s not just moped-riding watch thieves—there’s an illicit secondary market to be fed. Counterfeit watches are used in bait-and-switch scams where photos of a real watch are shown to a buyer who then ends up with the fake. The same trick is played on pawnbrokers, who are fed a string of legitimate watches before being duped by a knockoff.
According to a May 2025 report from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, the global fake goods trade was worth $467 billion in 2021—the most recent data available—and accounts for 2.3 percent of all global trade, rising to 4.7 percent in the European Union. Clothing, footwear, and leather goods are the most commonly seized counterfeit goods, while watches rank fifth by quantity, and first, comfortably, by value.
A second OECD report focused on Switzerland found that, also in 2021, around $4.7 billion worth of counterfeit goods infringed Swiss trademarks, leading to a $3 billion loss in domestic sales. More than 40 percent of those goods, by value, are watches, with roughly 65 percent of seizures originating in China and Hong Kong. Overall, the global fake Swiss watch market equates to about 7.7 percent of the value of Switzerland's legitimate watch exports, but with far lower production costs and sales prices per unit.
But remember, these figures are based on seized goods, not those that slip through the postal system unnoticed.
Imposter Syndrome
This should be black-and-white. Producing and selling counterfeit goods is a crime. The legality of buying, importing, and wearing them, however, varies by jurisdiction. Engaging in this industry can fairly be described as intellectual property theft, deceptive, and unethical.
One might question why buyers and wearers of counterfeit watches are pretending to be someone, or something, they aren’t. The options available for the budget watch collector have never been better. If they simply love watches, why not spend the same money on an interesting Seiko? Or, if a new genuine Rolex is beyond one’s budget, one of the brand’s certified pre-owned pieces offers an alternative to a collection of fakes.
The Reddit moderator we spoke to, who collects genuine luxury watches as well as replicas, says their love for these faux timepieces comes from being a watch fan. “I like the variety of watches that replicas allow me to have, and I like the ‘try before you buy’ that replicas afford me in some cases.”
Reddit’s own guidelines state that the selling or promoting of counterfeit goods may be considered a violation of the site’s trademark policy. The moderators of some other watch-centric subreddits have banned the discussion of counterfeit watches and parts, but for the communities reported here there seems to be little acknowledgment of wrongdoing.
In response to a request for comment, Reddit issued a statement to WIRED that says “counterfeit merchandise is covered by our Trademark Policy, which includes instructions for rightsholders who wish to file a report. We review and respond to all valid reports from rightsholders and take appropriate action on content that violates our policy.” Reddit’s Trademark Policy states that it “may ban users who repeatedly violate” it. “We may also ban subreddits after multiple removals of violative content or where it is clear that the subreddit is dedicated to violative content.”
Ultimately, what’s most striking isn’t merely the scale of this barely hiding counterfeit industry, but the misplaced enthusiasm driving it. These are real watch lovers who have built a genuine online community—people who are fluent in reference numbers, obsessing over index alignment and lume color. They are thrilled to share their knowledge and time, for free, with curious newcomers. It’s very much a genuine passion for watchmaking, but like the crooked hands of a red-lighted replica, it’s pointing the wrong way.
Our dive into the world of super clones showed us that something far more fundamental is at play here. We found that handling and wearing these timepieces brought near zero enjoyment. We love watches, from low-end to high. Buying your first Rolex or Omega, having saved for years, is a landmark achievement. It serves as a reminder of what the owner has managed to accomplish along the way—the destination of a hard-fought journey. A counterfeit, even one that looks so good it fools Rolex store staff and is classified as NWBIG by a stranger on Reddit, ultimately fails to offer joy that’s more than skin deep.

Russian envoy defends Hamas ties, says contacts helped free hostages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19

19:44:34 KST

Russian Ambassador to Israel Anatoly Viktorov has rejected public criticism in Israel over the Kremlin’s ties with Hamas, arguing that the contacts are intended to advance humanitarian solutions and have also helped efforts to secure the release of hostages. He also addressed ongoing cooperation between the two countries’ security agencies, contacts with the new Mossad chief and relations between Israel and Russia amid regional challenges.
In an interview with RTVI, a Russian-language television channel serving communities around the world, Viktorov said Moscow does not view Hamas as an organization created or supported by Russia and defended continued Russian contacts with representatives of the terrorist group. “Russia has never supported terrorist activity,” he said. “Hamas is not a product of Russian activity.”
According to Viktorov, Hamas is a product of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which he said continues because of the absence of a political solution to the Palestinian issue.
Viktorov also argued that cutting ties with the terrorist group would have prevented Russia from acting on humanitarian issues, particularly the hostages. He said a significant portion of Russia’s contacts with Hamas representatives since October 2023 had focused on helping secure the release of Israeli hostages, including Russian citizens.
The ambassador stressed that Russia does not accept Israel’s position on Hamas’ status but said that does not prevent Moscow from maintaining contacts with various Palestinian factions. He added that Russia supports the establishment of a Palestinian state living peacefully alongside Israel. “There is a chance for a political process, but the violence must stop,” he said.
Viktorov expressed support for moving to the next stage of the U.S. plan for the Gaza Strip but argued that the situation on the ground must first be stabilized and humanitarian issues addressed. He said any attempt to reach an agreement must be based on consent between the parties rather than a unilateral decision by an outside mediator.
He also rejected the idea that the United States alone could resolve the conflict, stressing the need for involvement by countries in the region and the broader international community.
Viktorov said Russia continues to maintain contacts with Palestinian factions in an effort to promote Palestinian political unity. Moscow, he said, wants that process to be based on the framework of the Palestine Liberation Organization, which he described as recognizing the importance of dialogue with Israel.
Ties with the new Mossad chief
The Russian ambassador also addressed the appointment of Roman Gofman as head of the Mossad. Viktorov said he knows Gofman personally and met him in his previous roles. He said he congratulated Gofman on the appointment and wished him success, while stressing the importance he places on continued ties between the two countries’ security services.
Viktorov said contacts between Russian and Israeli security agencies have not been severed and continue to address, among other issues, shared threats.
“We have things to discuss, experience to exchange and things to warn each other about,” he said, while declining to provide details about specific cooperation or warnings.
Viktorov also addressed the elections scheduled for Oct. 27, saying he does not expect them to bring a dramatic change in Israel-Russia relations. While the war between Russia and Ukraine remains a major issue for European countries, he said Russia is not at the center of Israel’s election campaign, where security and regional issues are more prominent.
The ambassador added that despite tensions between the two countries, political dialogue continues and Russia appreciates that Israel has not joined Western sanctions against Moscow or supplied lethal weapons to Ukraine.
Another issue Viktorov addressed was the resumption of direct flights between Israel and Russia. He said he hopes El Al will resume service to Russia and added that Moscow also wants Aeroflot flights to Israel restored.
Viktorov said Russia’s Red Wings currently operates direct flights to Israel but that the level of service is insufficient. He argued that Russia believes Aeroflot meets safety requirements and can resume flights to Israel.
Viktorov also addressed agricultural trade between the two countries, saying Russia remains a major supplier of grain to Israel and that Moscow does not expect cooperation in the sector to end.

A Hidden Holocaust Story From Lithuania's Forests Is Revealed in One Survivor's Diary
At the time of this printing, a few facts remain on which humanity can agree collectively: The sky is blue, the grass is green and the woods are spooky. "Into the woods, it's time to go," wrote Stephen Sondheim in his dark fairy-tale musical, "It may be all in vain, I know. Into the woods – but even so, I have to take the journey."
For Sondheim, the Grimm brothers' forests served as metaphor for our unknown futures, but for the Yiddish diarist Berl Kagan, who escaped from Lithuania's Kovno Ghetto, the woods were a real hideout from far worse people than any mythical witches, and a tentative place indeed.
"The forest was a place for thieves and robbers, a world far removed from Jews and the Jewish way of life," Kagan writes in his diary, "A Jew in the Woods," released in Max Rosenfeld's English translation this week from White Goat Press. "The forest threatens and terrorizes, and now – now we live in the forest, now we sleep in the forest, now the forest is our protector."
In Holocaust studies, the woods remain relatively mysterious versus other critical sites, like the camps and ghettos, where Nazi record-keepers archived their own depravity and Jewish prisoners risked their lives to document what they could of their unfolding catastrophe. In the decades after the war, the most famous accounts of the Holocaust would loom large in the public imagination: Anne Frank's attic and Elie Wiesel's harrowing account of Auschwitz, a site which stands today, annually hosting over a million visitors in 20 languages.

The Islamic Republic is establishing a new prosecutor’s office for “moral security” in Tehran to handle “violations and crimes against public morality,” including hijab non-compliance and social media posts critical of the regime, according to recordings released by Iranian media of Tehran Prosecutor Ali Salehi speaking at a meeting of the judiciary’s High Council.
He said the office’s first actions will include taking measures against stores selling “unconventional clothing” and monitoring cyberspace.
The office will reportedly be staffed by 12 judges.
Announcement comes amid the renewed presence of morality police
BBC Persian reported that the announcement comes amid the renewed presence of morality police and heightened street harassment of women perceived to be violating Iran’s compulsory dress code, including women seen with their hair uncovered or wearing short sleeves.
Salehi alleged the office had already helped in the arrest of two influencers who, according to him, had “mocked” the Arbaeen ceremonies (a religious ceremony marking the 40th day of mourning for Imam Hussein) online.
"Today, the Special Prosecutor's Office for Moral Security in Tehran is seriously following up on issues and cases in this area with its concerned judges; the monitoring unit located in this prosecutor's office is also continuously reviewing content published in cyberspace so that legal action can be taken against those who publish immoral content," he said. "In this regard, recently, following the publication of an offensive video regarding the Arbaeen ceremony of Husseini in cyberspace by a woman and a man, the issue was immediately placed on the agenda of the Tehran Prosecutor's Office, and by order of the judicial authority, their page in cyberspace was blocked, and the defendants were arrested and detained."
Social media users were made to publish apology videos on their accounts
An animal-rights influencer was reportedly arrested for using a religious song, "Let's Go to Najaf," which had been associated with the ceremonies, in a video of herself feeding stray dogs, according to BBC Persian.
Notably, several social media users were made to publish apology videos on their accounts for posts relating to support for the exiled crown prince or Mahsa Amini, a young Kurdish woman who was murdered in 2022 after being abducted by the morality police for wearing the hijab incorrectly.
Despite Salehi’s comments, the Iranian legal network Dadbaan insisted in a statement that “merely publishing content in cyberspace or choosing a type of attire cannot, without the existence of explicit legal provisions and the fulfillment of the elements of a crime, serve as the basis for detention, blocking accounts, or imposing restrictions on citizens. The legal principle of the legality of crimes and punishments also requires that vague titles such as ‘moral security’ not be turned into tools for expanding the scope of criminal intervention in private life and freedom of expression.
“Crackdowns on attire, lifestyle, business activities, and published content in cyberspace have previously become one of the methods of exerting social pressure on citizens. The expansion of constant monitoring and judicial action in this area signals the transformation of the criminal justice system into a tool for controlling everyday behaviors and social suppression, further restricting privacy and individual freedoms.”

First 1,400 housing units to be marketed in controversial E1 area of West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:35:06 UTC
19:35:06 KST

The government plan to populate the contentious E1 area, located between Ma’aleh Adumim and Jerusalem, moved one step closer to fruition this week, when Ma’aleh Adumim Mayor Guy Yifrach announced the launch of the area’s first 1,400 housing units.
“This is tremendous news for Ma’aleh Adumim, and major news for the State of Israel as a whole,” said Yifrach in a statement on Tuesday announcing the upcoming marketing of the units.
The E1 corridor is comprised of some 12 square kilometers inside the jurisdictional boundaries of Ma’aleh Adumim, and any construction there would become part of the existing settlement city.
Plans approved by the Civil Administration’s Higher Planning Committee in August 2025 would see 3,412 housing units ultimately built in E1, which would increase Ma’aleh Adumim’s population, already one of the largest Jewish cities in the West Bank, by some 12,000 from its current 38,000.
Thanking Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Defense Minister Israel Katz and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, Yifrach said, “The construction of the E1 neighborhood is vital to the future of Ma’aleh Adumim, to its continued growth, expansion, and the strengthening of its position as a strong city in Israel.
“We have come a long way to reach this moment. There were obstacles, there were delays, and there were those who thought it would never happen. But we believed, we persevered, we took action, and we never gave up.”
E1 construction faced decades of US opposition over West Bank location
Yifrach was referring to the decades-long opposition against building in the region by successive US administrations prior to US President Donald Trump, due to the area’s sensitive location that provides a corridor between the southern and northern West Bank.
Ma’aleh Adumim, some eight kilometers from Jerusalem, is in the national consensus of remaining part of Israel if an eventual Palestinian state is ever established.
But E1 has proved far more contentious.
The plan to build the area was first developed by the Shamir government in 1991 and advanced by the Rabin government in the mid-1990s in an effort to create Israeli territorial contiguity around Jerusalem.
The plan was halted under the Rabin administration due to American objections, which have remained constant since then. There have been periodic attempts to revive the plan, including by prime minister Ariel Sharon in 2004, but opposition from the US and the European Union had continued to shut down the efforts.
When Smotrich approved building on E1 last summer, he said it would provide the final nail in the coffin of aspirations for a Palestinian state.
“From the Palestinian perspective and that of the international community, this is a critical area. Without it, the establishment of a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital is simply impossible,” he said at the time.
“Those around the world who try to recognize a Palestinian state will see our response on the ground – not with documents or declarations, but with facts: homes, roads, and Jewish families building their lives here. They will talk about a Palestinian dream – and we will continue to build a Jewish reality,” he said. “This reality buries the idea for good – there is nothing to recognize,” Smotrich added.
EU foreign policy chief Kallas says E1 plan would divide West Bank
Following Smotrich’s announcement, European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said that the E1 plan undermines the two-state solution, and, if implemented, would “permanently cut the geographical and territorial contiguity between occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank and sever the connection between the northern and southern West Bank.”
In March 2025, the security cabinet approved the building of a new road which would connect the Palestinian villages of Za’ayyem and Eizariya near Ma’aleh Adumim and would provide an alternative solution for Palestinians to drive between the northern and southern West Bank.
Detractors say that the road will not be enough to prevent Israel from effectively blocking a Palestinian state from having any contiguity. Undeterred, Yifrah lauded the upcoming campaign to sell the first homes in E1.
“The first 1,400 housing units are only the beginning,” he said. “We will continue to build, develop, expand, and move Ma’aleh Adumim forward.”
UK Foreign Office condemned project, summoned Israeli Charge d'Affaires
"This Israeli Government’s publication of a tender for the E1 settlement project is an unacceptable and destructive act," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement on Wednesday evening.
"Today, I made clear to the Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar that the Israeli Government must halt E1 plans immediately, retract the tender and stop all settlement expansion," he said.
"In addition, the Israeli Chargé d’Affaires has been summoned to the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office, where we set out the UK’s profound objection to this move by the Netanyahu government and demanded an immediate reversal."

More than a ride: Why Copenhagen’s cyan taxis are redefining the professional driver experience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:31:13 UTC
19:31:13 KST

If you have spent any time in the streets of Copenhagen recently, you have likely noticed the distinctive cyan-colored electric vehicles weaving through the city traffic. These are more than just a colorful addition to the cityscape; they represent a fundamental shift in the Danish taxi industry. Green SM is entering the market with a “driver-first” philosophy, built on the belief that a high-quality passenger experience is impossible without a professional, well-supported driver behind the wheel.
A new standard for working conditions
The traditional taxi model often relies on independent contractors working long, unpredictable hours on commission. Green SM has turned this model on its head by acting as a direct employer, offering Danish contracts and a fixed hourly wage. This provides drivers with the financial security and stability often missing in the transport sector.
Mehmet, a driver who recently transitioned to the Green SM team, highlights the impact of this change on his daily life.
“I chose Green SM because there are much better working conditions,” he explains.
For Mehmet, the most significant change is the shift from grueling 12-hour days to manageable 8-hour shifts.
“It means a lot to me because I was driving 12 hours every day before (…) Now it is 7.5 to 8 hours. So you are much fresher and well-rested,” he says.
This shift ensures that drivers are well-rested, alert, and capable of providing the safe, attentive service that the company promises.
Professionalism through intensive training
Green SM does not just provide a car and a contract; they invest heavily in their team. Every driver undergoes comprehensive training that covers both technical driving skills and “five-star” customer care. This includes everything from maintaining a neat, professional appearance to mastering the nuances of passenger privacy and courtesy.
This commitment to training is visible the moment a Green SM taxi pulls up to the curb. Mehmet notes that the training has fundamentally changed his approach to the job.
“We are more professional now. Before, we never opened the door for customers. Now we have started opening the door. There is much better service at Green SM,” he explains.
This focus on standardized quality ensures that whether you are heading to a business meeting or Kastrup Airport, the level of service remains consistently high.
The silent, green advantage
Beyond the social and professional standards, Green SM operates a 100% electric fleet. This choice supports Copenhagen’s goals for a more livable city by reducing both CO2 emissions and noise pollution. For the driver, the electric fleet offers a vastly improved workspace.
A quiet, smooth-running vehicle reduces the fatigue associated with engine vibration and noise, creating a calmer environment for both the driver and the passenger.
Mehmet has noticed a palpable shift in the internal team culture since his shift – a much better workplace and a real sense of belonging: “The colleagues are very happy, actually. We aren’t grumpy anymore; now we are a team.”
Copenhagen is taking notice
The “Professional Driver Experience” is not just internal corporate talk, passengers are actively acknowledging the difference
Mehmet shares that his passengers often comment on the improved standards. “Most people talk to me and say, ‘Finally, you have a good job now.’ They can tell right away that the working conditions have gotten better,” he says and shares that there is a growing sense among locals that a driver who is treated well is a driver who will get them home more safely and comfortably.
For those looking to experience the “cyan difference” Green SM offers full transparency through its app, which shows the price of a trip before booking and issues automatic electronic receipts. To celebrate their launch, the company is currently offering 25% off the first five rides booked through the app.
As Copenhagen continues to move toward a more sustainable and integrated transport future, Green SM’s focus on the professional driver serves as a reminder that in the world of mobility, the person behind the wheel is just as important as the vehicle they drive.

Dell XPS 13 vs. MacBook Neo: A Surprising Upset
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Ever since the MacBook Neo was announced this spring, I've been looking for a serious alternative. Not a cheap knockoff that sacrifices quality for price. No, no. I was hunting for a Windows laptop with the same goal as the MacBook Neo—hiding its compromises and delivering an otherwise premium laptop at a lower cost. For months, it was crickets.
Then, the Dell XPS 13 showed up on my doorstep, and it understood the assignment. For many reasons, this was the one I'd been waiting for. But the question remains: Is it actually the better budget laptop? The answer surprised me when I dug into the testing.
Hidden Compromises
When the MacBook Neo was originally announced, it was a shocker. Apple coming in at the $599 price point for the base configuration felt unreal. Apple had never in its history brought the MacBook to such a low price. Even at its new $699 starting price, it's in unprecedented territory. Importantly, this encroached on the territory of Windows laptops, where it has traditionally had a monopoly.
And while many Windows laptops are available at this price, they suffer from many of the same problems, such as cheap materials or corners cut with low-quality displays and touchpads. Even a cheap laptop I like quite a bit, like the HP OmniBook 5 (with the Snapdragon X Plus), has a weak point in its touchpad.
But the Dell XPS 13 sought to match the MacBook Neo's premium quality in nearly every aspect. It has the same starting price of $699 (or $599 for students). It's exactly the same size at just a half-inch thick, so when the lid is closed and you're holding it, it feels just as portable. The XPS 13 weighs 2.2 pounds, half a pound lighter than the MacBook Neo. The Neo isn't heavy, but holding both in your hands, the difference is noticeable. That's the first point in favor of the XPS 13.
Despite a slightly smaller screen (13 inches, measured diagonally), the MacBook Neo sits taller than the XPS 13 when the lid is open. That's because the XPS 13's 13.4-inch display is surrounded by much smaller bezels—particularly the bottom, which gives the XPS 13 a more modern look. The white keyboard and flashier color options of the MacBook Neo certainly have their appeal, especially since the XPS 13 comes in only two shades of silver. But in general, more screen real estate and smaller dimensions are preferable, especially if you want to travel on an airplane with your laptop.
And then there's the screen itself. Most $700 laptops have mediocre screens that aren't bright enough and have poor colors. I never expected Apple to skimp on the display, of course, and it didn't. It goes up to 509 nits (as tested) and has decent color reproduction. But the XPS 13 is better in three ways. First, it has a touchscreen, which MacBooks don't (yet) have. That's a nice addition for an entry-level model. It also has a 120-Hz refresh rate, which gives the screen fast, fluid responsiveness that not even the MacBook Air has. Again, that's a feature that's exceedingly rare to find on a budget-level laptop. Lastly, the XPS 13 has better color saturation, specifically on the Adobe RGB and P3 color scales. It's actually one of the better IPS screens I've tested on a laptop, and it's as sharp as the MacBook Neo.
None of these are weak points of the MacBook Neo, but it's worth noting that the XPS 13 has it beat in a number of these areas. That's also true of the keyboard and trackpad. Both are excellent on these laptops, and I found myself comfortable using them right off the bat. Again, trackpads in particular can be a sore spot for budget Windows laptops, but Dell smartly didn't skimp on it. Apple's the one that compromised on the keyboard, both by not including Touch ID in the base model and by removing backlighting (which the XPS 13 includes).
Ports, Storage, and Videoconferencing
I already mentioned the display and the portability, but there are a few other places where the XPS 13 is the clear winner. The first is the USB-C ports. Both devices have two, but the XPS 13 splits them, so one is on the left side, and one is on the right side. I really like this decision, as it allows you to charge the device from either side. Then, there's the speed of these USB-C ports. One of the USB-C ports on the MacBook Neo is an outdated USB 2 port. Not only is it slow for file transfers, but it also can't natively output to an external display. Both USB-C ports on the XPS 13 are USB 3.2 Gen 2, which can each support a 4K display and transfer data at up to 10 Gbps.
The Neo does have an advantage when it comes to ports, though. It has a headphone jack, whereas the XPS 13 doesn't. This might be less of a big deal today than it was in the past, but I prefer laptops to keep them.
The XPS 13 comes with 512 GB of storage in both the base and upgraded models. The MacBook Neo base model comes only with 256 GB, and you'll need to upgrade to the Touch ID model for 521 GB. On top of that, Dell's laptop uses faster storage. That's a winning combination.
The videoconferencing setup is similarly good. Both webcams are 1080p. Though the image processing is a bit better on the MacBook Neo, the XPS 13 includes an IR camera for logging in without a password. The base configuration of the Neo doesn't have Touch ID, so you have to type a password to log in, change settings, and pay online.
The RAM Problem
Apple never claimed the MacBook Neo was a powerhouse. Built on an iPhone chip (the A18 Pro) and limited to 8 GB of RAM, it is clearly designed for college students and anyone with lower-level computing needs. When I tested it initially, I found that if I wasn't paying attention, it was easy to let open applications, tons of browser tabs, and background tasks slow the computer down, with the main bottleneck being the 8 GB of RAM. Apple hasn't sold a MacBook with 8 GB of RAM since 2024, but the company has always insisted that its unified memory system means it doesn't need as much capacity as a Windows PC. But is that really true? Now that we have a very comparable Windows system with 8 GB of RAM as well, it'll be easy to test just how true Apple's claims are.
The bad news is that both devices took very little effort to use up the available memory. Playing a YouTube video with various news sites open in six Google Chrome tabs was enough to use over 90 percent of the 8 GB. Neither Windows nor macOS feels optimized for a computer with just 8 GB of RAM these days, no doubt from all the AI-infused tasks running in the background. Now, just because you're getting dangerously close to reaching 100 percent of the memory utilization, that doesn't mean your computer instantly freezes up. It takes a lot to get these systems to grind to a halt, but with a 16-GB laptop, you'll spend much less time managing what tabs and applications you have open. On the other hand, if you're a student coming from a cheap Chromebook or hand-me-down computer, these laptops will feel like a nice upgrade.
The XPS 13 has a fan inside, while the MacBook Neo is passively cooled. Under a heavy load you can hear that fan spin up in the XPS 13, whereas the Neo is completely silent. Both laptops get excellent battery life—enough to get through a full day of class or work. That's another area where laptops at this price tended to suffer in the past.
But the big difference between these two laptops is how you can configure them. Both start at $700 ($699 for the Neo, to be exact), and you get one upgrade option. For an extra $100, you can move up to the MacBook Neo with 512 GB of storage and Touch ID built in. On the other hand, the Dell XPS 13 has a $900 model that's identical to the base model, except it has 16 GB of RAM. So yes, the 16-GB version of the XPS 13 is $100 more expensive. But it's better in nearly every way, and it's likely the best laptop you can buy for less than $1,000.
And even when comparing the 8-GB model, the XPS 13 handily beats the MacBook Neo in tons of small ways. It has a better display, a backlit keyboard, two USB ports—one on each side—that support charging and 4K monitors, and it's more portable. It does all that while looking super sharp and feeling just as premium as the Neo. While I think everyone should buy a 16-GB laptop, at the 8-GB level, the Dell XPS 13 is the better laptop no matter how you slice it.
