====================================================================================================

Bennett unveils election security plan: hit Iran for Hezbollah fire, declare Qatar an enemy state
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:50:36 UTC
18:50:36 KST

Former prime minister and Beyachad chairman Naftali Bennett unveiled his security doctrine Wednesday ahead of the election, arguing that the October 7 massacre exposed not only a failure along the Gaza border but the collapse of an entire security concept fostered for years under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
“What collapsed on October 7 was not only the defensive line facing Gaza,” Bennett said at a party conference. “On October 7, an entire security doctrine collapsed, one that Netanyahu had instilled for years.”
Bennett said he intends to “break four assumptions” if elected to lead the next government.
The first, he said, concerns Iran and Hezbollah. Against what he described as the existing equation under which Iran responds to Israeli strikes in Lebanon, Bennett proposed reversing the logic: “Every Hezbollah attack will lead to us striking Iran.”
He also repeated a position he previously presented at the ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth conference, saying that while Netanyahu has described Qatar as a “complex country,” he would formally define it as an enemy state.
“Anyone who does not understand that after October 7 is not fit to lead Israel,” Bennett said.
A third assumption, he argued, is that Turkey and Qatar should have a role in Gaza’s postwar arrangements and in the Board of Peace.
“We will remove Turkey and Qatar from Gaza and bring Egypt in instead, while preserving freedom of action in Gaza,” he said.
Bennett also addressed the roughly half a million illegal weapons he said are circulating inside Israel. He pledged to redefine the issue as a national security threat rather than a criminal one, bringing in the IDF and Shin Bet and declaring areas with illegal weapons closed military zones until they are cleared.
“The October 7 government is still captive to the assumptions of October 6,” Bennett said.
He contrasted that with his own previous government, arguing that it changed Israel’s deterrence equation with Gaza.
“After tens of thousands of rockets and incendiary balloons that Netanyahu’s government contained, we hit them even over a single balloon,” Bennett said, claiming his government delivered southern communities their quietest year in years.
Bennett also addressed the IDF manpower crisis, saying it was untenable for the military to be short 20,000 soldiers while around 100,000 healthy young Haredi men remained outside military service.
“In the next government under my leadership, we will draft everyone,” he said. “No exemptions and no tricks.”
He also criticized remarks by former Shin Bet chief Yoram Cohen, who is affiliated with Gadi Eisenkot’s party, that the party could accept exemptions for 30% of young Haredi men.
“The moment you start with ideas like a 30% exemption, committees and frameworks, we have all been there,” Bennett said. “And we know from experience exactly how it ends.”
After Bennett, his No. 2, Yair Lapid, presented what he described as Beyachad’s top foreign policy goals for the next government.
“The diplomatic crisis was created not only because of circumstances, but also because of the negligence, arrogance and amateurism of the Israeli government,” Lapid said. He also opposed giving up U.S. military aid to Israel, calling Netanyahu’s position “a serious mistake.”
Lapid laid out six goals for repairing Israel’s foreign relations, beginning with the United States. He said Israel must restore the bipartisan standing it enjoyed until recent years, rebuild ties with the European Union, deepen cooperation with NATO and confront hostile public opinion in countries including Spain, France and Ireland.
He also called for repairing relations with Diaspora Jewry. “World Jewry is our family,” Lapid said. “It is also a strategic and diplomatic asset that we need to preserve.”
Lapid said Israel should deepen its regional integration, with Egypt and the United Arab Emirates as key partners, while making normalization with Saudi Arabia a central objective. At the same time, he said Israel must prevent uranium enrichment on Saudi soil “at any cost.”
Echoing Bennett, Lapid called for Qatar to be declared an enemy state. On Turkey, however, he struck a more cautious tone, saying Israel should explore whether tensions can be lowered. “This confrontation is not good for us,” he said.
His final priorities were better coordination between economic policy and foreign policy, and an overhaul of Israel’s international public diplomacy. Israel’s voice abroad, he said, must be professional, attuned to younger audiences and effective on social media.
“A lot more Noa Tishby,” Lapid said, “a lot less Orit Strock.”
First published: 12:50, 08.19.26

Ukrainian parliament appoints Andrii Sybiha as foreign minister
The Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian Parliament) has appointed acting Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha as the new Minister of Foreign Affairs.
Source: parliamentary session on 19 August
Details: The decision was supported by 266 MPs.
Quote from Sybiha: "We are at a decisive stage of the war. A stage at which diplomacy in particular is taking on special significance. This places a special responsibility on all of us... There is nothing more important than ending the war. Much has been done over the past year... But as long as the war continues... We work together, because there is strength in unity."
Details: Sybiha also added that he views the appointment as "an enormous challenge and an enormous responsibility".
Following the vote, Sybiha also took the oath of office.
Background:
- On 12 July, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the Cabinet of Ministers needed to be reshuffled and announced changes to the leadership of law enforcement agencies. On 14 July, the Verkhovna Rada approved the resignation of Yuliia Svyrydenko as prime minister. As a result, the entire government resigned.
- The dismissal of Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, which many people considered unjustified, has sparked public discontent. Since 16 July, protests demanding Fedorov's reinstatement have been held almost daily in many cities across the country.
- On 17 July, the Cabinet of Ministers appointed Yevhenii Khmara as acting defence minister and Andrii Sybiha as acting foreign minister.
- On 18 August, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy submitted motions to parliament to appoint Yevhenii Khmara as defence minister and Andrii Sybiha as foreign minister.

UP flood situation under watch: 173 villages affected, over 4,800 shifted to safer areas

UP flood situation under watch: 173 villages affected, over 4,800 shifted to safer areas
Newsdesk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 19, 2026, 15:16 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath
Uttar Pradesh authorities have intensified flood relief and rescue operations across 13 districts, with 173 villages affected and 4,845 people shifted to safer locations as the state government keeps a close watch on rising river levels and vulnerable areas.The government has deployed 16 National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) teams, State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) personnel and Provincial Armed Constabulary (PAC) teams across the state, while 724 medical teams and 534 ambulances have been placed on duty for emergency response and healthcare services.The Relief Commissioner's Office said 13,058 hectares of land and 84,362 people have been affected by the floods so far. The administration has established 1,589 flood outposts and prepared 1,263 flood shelters, of which 41 are currently in use and accommodating 1,045 people.
13 districts affected, river levels monitored
The affected districts are Badaun, Bahraich, Ballia, Barabanki, Bijnor, Farrukhabad, Gautam Buddh Nagar, Gonda, Kasganj, Lakhimpur Kheri, Muzaffarnagar, Sitapur and Unnao.The state government said the overall flood situation is currently under control, but several rivers are flowing at or above danger levels, prompting continued monitoring and preparedness in vulnerable districts.The Ghaghra near Elgin Bridge in Barabanki is flowing above the danger mark, while the Ganga has reached the danger mark at Kachhla Bridge in Badaun and Fatehgarh in Farrukhabad.
The Sharda river at Palia Kalan and Shardanagar in Lakhimpur Kheri, and the Ghaghra at Ayodhya and Turtipar in Ballia, are also flowing around the danger mark.District administrations in these areas have been kept on alert, with officials instructed to monitor river levels and respond to any deterioration in the situation.Relief Commissioner Dr Hrishikesh Bhaskar Yashod reviewed the flood situation and ongoing relief and rescue operations on Tuesday. He directed district magistrates to move affected residents to relief camps or other safe locations wherever necessary.Officials have also been instructed to ensure adequate supplies of food, medical facilities and essential relief material, while keeping flood outposts operational.
Relief operations expanded across affected areas
The administration has deployed 428 boats and motor boats along with 1,101 local divers to support rescue operations.So far, 15,238 food-grain packets and 30,316 meal packets have been distributed among flood-affected people.The government has also directed officials to ensure adequate availability of rescue teams and equipment and to activate additional resources immediately if the situation requires.The Control Room at the Relief Commissioner's Office is maintaining contact with district officials and monitoring information received from flood-affected areas. Complaints and requests received through the 1070 helpline are being acted upon, according to the government.
724 medical teams deployed
Healthcare arrangements have been strengthened in the affected areas, with 724 medical teams and 534 ambulances available across the state.Authorities said 19,406 people have received medical treatment so far, while anti-snake venom has been provided to 566 people.To support public health measures, 43,612 chlorine tablets and 23,476 ORS packets have been distributed. Larvicide has also been sprayed in 1,468 villages to help prevent mosquito-borne diseases.The administration has also made arrangements for livestock affected by the floods. According to the government, 6,067 animals have been affected so far.A total of 208 quintals of fodder has been distributed, while 11,465 sick animals have received treatment. More than 4.04 lakh animals have also been vaccinated.
NDRF, SDRF and PAC teams on standby
Sixteen NDRF teams have been deployed across Uttar Pradesh to deal with emergency situations. SDRF teams are operating in various districts, while PAC personnel have been deployed in 52 districts.The administration has been instructed to deploy additional rescue teams and resources wherever required.A joint team of the Uttar Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority and the United Nations Development Programme has also conducted field inspections in Basti, Siddharthnagar, Sant Kabir Nagar, Sant Kabir Nagar, Azamgarh, Mau and Ballia.The team reviewed flood shelters, model flood shelters, relief kits, rescue and relief teams and preparedness measures in affected villages.Ministers in charge and local public representatives have also been conducting field visits to assess the situation and relief arrangements.
140.52 crore SMS alerts sent
The state government has placed emphasis on early warnings and public communication as part of its flood management measures.
According to the Relief Commissioner's Office, 140.52 crore SMS alerts were sent between August 1 and August 18 to communicate weather department warnings to residents.Information on flood prevention and safety measures is also being shared through social media.The state control room is maintaining continuous communication with district officials and monitoring flood-related developments. Information received from the districts is being used to track relief and rescue operations and identify areas requiring immediate intervention.The administration is also monitoring river water levels and maintaining the availability of boats, motor boats, rescue teams and other resources.With several rivers still at or above danger levels, authorities have kept vulnerable districts on alert despite describing the overall flood situation as under control.

Hot or Not Built the Internet We’re Still Swiping Through
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

Before the internet learned to like, match, and swipe, it learned to ask one brutally simple question: hot or not?
Launched in 2000, Hot or Not invited people to upload photographs of themselves and be rated by strangers on a scale from 1 to 10. It was crude, addictive, and, within weeks, one of the most visited sites on the web. More importantly, it turned an intensely subjective judgment—whether someone was attractive—into structured data that could be ranked, compared, and used to organize human behavior.
Twenty-six years later, the dating industry appears to be retreating from the internet Hot or Not helped create. Earlier this month, Bumble founder and chief executive Whitney Wolfe Herd said the company was moving away from its swipe format toward “fewer, better, more considered signals.” A day earlier, Match Group, the company behind Tinder, said that the app will introduce more in-person events by the end of the year.
Tinder Events was launched earlier this year, offering offline experiences in response to its declining user base. The more immediate plan is to expand into 26 cities worldwide by the end of September.
After a quarter-century spent optimizing how we rate and reject one another, the internet may finally be experiencing hotness fatigue. Dating apps are struggling inside a culture saturated with the behavior Hot or Not helped standardize: the endless loop of judging other people while volunteering to be judged ourselves.
About Face
In the early 2000s, submitting your photograph to the open internet was still unusual. Hot or Not asked people to volunteer their own faces and allow strangers, at scale, to determine their fate.
In 2000, this was groundbreaking stuff. Not because people were more sensitive back then, but because putting your own photograph on the open web was still pretty deviant behavior.
The site, conceived by founders James Hong and Jim Young, became one of the most trafficked sites on the internet within weeks. Not to mention, this was one of the first cases where human judgment could be converted into structured data, and structured data could then be used to organize human behavior.
“The design itself gamified physical attractiveness, while helping to normalize the type of ranking, rating, and scoring that is now endemic to social media,” says Brooke Erin Duffy, professor in the Department of Communication at Cornell University.
Public scrutiny of appearance traces way back to the offline days of paparazzi culture and gossip columns in tabloid print media. What Hot or Not changed, thanks to the internet, was that it let ordinary people volunteer for the microscope.
Duffy’s phrase for it is that people could now “willingly thrust themselves under a high-powered lens,” and that willingness itself was the innovation, the one every platform since has monetized.
From Rating to Swiping
Hot or Not’s “Meet Me,” the paid matchmaking feature the founders added in 2001, introduced the concept of the mutual opt-in (meaning neither party could message the other until both had expressed interest).
This was later the very mechanism Tinder was built on, though it combined it with the concept of the rating loop. The swipe is the score and the match at once.
Tinder has long been reported and criticized for having an internal desirability rating for every user, an invisible ranking that shapes the algorithm. At least Hot or Not had the decency to tell you your score.
Treena Orchard, associate professor in the School of Health Studies at Western University and a long-standing critic of dating app design, says “the success of swipe culture on dating apps reflects our willingness to be seduced by tech promises of easy, efficient fun, when in reality what these apps have done is drive a wedge between human beings, to our profound detriment.”
She traces a broader inheritance too, one that goes well past dating. Hot or Not, in her reading, cultivated an insatiable digital appetite for the public consumption of personal information, and ushered in an era where beauty and body standards were set by anyone with a computer. “It ignited something new that can never be put back in the proverbial bottle,” she says.
And the parallel with putting yourself up to be rated on Hot or Not back then, and putting yourself online nowadays, is a shared willingness to open ourselves up to be judged, roasted, and subjected to online vitriol.
The Prototype Everyone Copied
Hot or Not can, however, be let off on a technicality, and Hong himself has made the argument over the years that the site did not create such an appetite for judgment—it merely gave it a platform. It was an attractive model to copy. YouTube’s founders said that a first draft of the site in 2005 was pretty much Hot or Not for video.
FaceMash, Mark Zuckerberg’s 2003 Harvard imitation (that people now misremember as the same thing), scraped student photographs—without permission—and pitted them against each other. At least Hot or Not was honest in its approach. Hong has also said the company gave free hosting to ZipDash (which later became Google’s mobile maps) and to a young Twitter.
And though it existed to rank people’s attractiveness, it actually helped incubate parts of the infrastructure of the internet that eventually made rating everything normal.
Hot or Not itself didn’t survive the internet it helped design. It couldn’t compete with free, ad-funded rivals, was sold to the company behind Ashley Madison in 2008, and was eventually offloaded to Badoo, which relaunched it in 2014 as, of all things, a Tinder-style swiping app.
Hot or Not was, at its core, an early prototype for the participatory internet, where the user became both the product and the judge. Twenty-six years later, the same internet is discovering the uncomfortable inverse: that the whole loop business of liking, rating, swiping, and validating is actually starting to eat itself.
This story originally appeared in WIRED Middle East.

Drought forces Swiss cows to descend early from Alpine pastures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:43:57 UTC
18:43:57 KST

Drought forces Swiss cows to descend early from Alpine pastures
Some Swiss farmers have already brought their livestock down from the mountain pastures earlier than planned due to drought conditions.
The Jura Arc, French-speaking Switzerland and parts of eastern Switzerland have been particularly hard hit, said Selina Droz, director-general of the Swiss Alpine Economy Federation (FSEA). The situation is critical across the whole country.
+ Why Swiss cows climb mountains
The FSEA does not have precise figures on the number of farms that have had to bring forward the descent from the mountain pastures. According to Droz, the vast majority of the mountain pastures affected have, however, brought only some of their animals back down to the valley, in order to conserve drinking water and fodder there too.
This year’s “highly exceptional situation” is also taking its toll on lowland farms, whose fodder reserves are equally limited due to the drought. The only alternative is the early slaughter of livestock, a measure to which some have already resorted.
The shorter summer grazing period is also having an impact on production. The FSEA forecasts below-average production of alpine cheese for the current year. For Gruyère d’alpage, for example, the trade association expects a drop in production of around 10% compared with the previous year.
More
The difficult search for real Swiss cows
Given climate change, dry summers are set to become more frequent in the future. However, early descents from the alpine pastures must remain an emergency measure. According to Droz, transporting water by road or helicopter only makes sense if, for example, the farm in question has even less fodder available.
All alpine farms should therefore review their own water infrastructure and adapt it where necessary. The implementation of projects such as new reservoirs or the tapping of springs requires further funding from the Confederation and the cantons.
According to the FSEA, Switzerland has around 6,600 alpine pastures, of which around a third of the usable agricultural area is farmed in summer, producing 5,500 tonnes of alpine cheese each year.

18:42:00 KST

GOMEL, 19 August (BelTA) - An exchange of prisoners of war between Russia and Ukraine was conducted on the territory of Belarus, BelTA has learned.
Belarus continues to fulfill its humanitarian mission and once again served as a place for the prisoner exchange. Russia and Ukraine swapped over 103 people each.
Anton from the Irkutsk Oblast of Russia also did not hide his emotions. He is returning home after an endlessly long 20 months. In September, his daughter Sofia will start school. Hers was the first voice he heard on the phone. He was breathless with emotion. “I’ve missed everyone so much! I love you all! When I get to Moscow, I’ll call,” he said. The man hopes to walk his daughter to her first day of school together with his wife.
A prisoner of war, Viktor, carefully clutches in his hands a file with photographs of his children and loved ones. The man is heading to Tula, where a large family is waiting to welcome him. He has five children. A daughter, Anzhelina, and four sons, each of whose names begin with the letter M – Mikhail, Maksim, Matvey, and Miron. By the way, he has not yet met his youngest in person, having only seen him in photographs. The baby was born when the father was already far from home. “I read and reread these letters 10-20 times. It gave me strength,” he said.
Words of gratitude also came from the Commissioner for Human Rights in the Russian Federation, Yana Lantratova. She thanked the Belarusians for the safe corridor, and the Ukrainian colleagues for the constructive dialogue. “It is important that for the first time in a long time, 31 wounded people are being exchanged. They are in various conditions. These are the guys whose mothers, wives, and sisters came to ask personally. Their families and loved ones are very, very much waiting for them. Today, during the journey, I had numerous calls from mothers who asked me about their health. We went through the buses, the ambulances, and talked to them. Many thanks to the Belarusian side, which is helping us conduct this exchange today,” she said.
She said that a routine has been established to keep track of all inquiries from both sides. “We have agreed that we go to see prisoners of war. Since our last meeting, we have visited 618 Ukrainian prisoners of war to check on their conditions of detention. This is truly very important. The same is done by Dmitry Valeryevich [Lubinets, the Commissioner for Human Rights of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine] and his team with regard to our guys,” the Ombudswoman stated.
The ombudspersons of Russia and Ukraine also exchanged a large number of letters from relatives and loved ones for prisoners of war on both sides. “This is very important. I know how they are looking forward to receive these letters and how much they mean to them,” Yana Lantratova emphasized. She noted that one of the letters she delivered to a prisoner of war during her last visit contained photographs of his newborn grandson. “The man was overjoyed,” she added.
Work continues on mutual humanitarian exchanges in both directions, the ombudsman assured. “There is also a great deal of work on mutual document exchanges. At the previous meeting, we noted that this process had been launched - a very large number of requests are coming to the offices of ombudsmen in both countries. And today we have already exchanged documents. This means that people will be able to receive the payments, benefits, or other assistance they need to protect their rights. We are continuing this work. Today we discussed the next exchanges. We hope that family reunifications, the transfer of civilians, and prisoner exchanges will take place more frequently between our sides,” Yana Lantratova said.
A number of issues were constructively discussed, the main one being the return of citizens from various categories on both sides, Dmitry Lubinets confirmed. “This includes the return of prisoners of war and the intensification of exchange processes. The second category is civilians who are on the territory of both Ukraine and the Russian Federation. A separate issue is the return of elderly and peaceful citizens. We recently had another humanitarian exchange,” he said.
Constant monitoring of detention conditions for prisoners of war was discussed in detail. “We have agreed that this will be done on an ongoing, systematic basis. We will exchange information after such monitoring. We pay special attention to where prisoners receive meals, how medical care is provided, and how their rights to religious observance are ensured,” the Ukrainian Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights outlined.
This work never stops, the two ombudsmen assured, noting that meetings and discussions are not always public. “The most important thing is when we see concrete results,” Dmitry Lubinets emphasized.Irina Kostevich, Chairperson of the Standing Committee on Labor and Social Affairs of the House of Representatives, was also present at the Belarusian-Ukrainian border area. She stressed that another truly important step had been taken. “Belarus is carrying out a very important humanitarian mission. For several years now, a humanitarian platform has been operating here on the instruction of Belarusian President Aleksandr Lukashenko. Today, another humanitarian mission has been carried out. What is its significance, why is it important? The process is ongoing, with regular exchanges in place. Today, the human rights ombudsmen of both Russia and Ukraine are taking part in this platform. A productive dialogue has taken place, and certain cooperation frameworks have been developed - for parcels, for exchanging letters, and for monitoring the whereabouts of prisoners of war. A plan for further exchange actions has also been outlined,” she said. She also noted that words of gratitude were addressed to Belarus. “Today, such a comfortable corridor is being provided, not only in terms of logistics. It is a reliable corridor, an island of safety, as it is now being called,” she added.
Irina Kostevich walked through the buses carrying Russian and Ukrainian prisoners of war. “On behalf of all of Belarus, I received words of gratitude. They thanked us for the cleanliness and warmth of the Belarusian people, for the hot meals, and for the medical care that those in need received promptly. Many said that while traveling through Belarusian land, they felt at home,” she said.
“We will certainly continue this mission. Belarusians are committed to peace and friendship. We very much hope that peace will come soon to both Russia and Ukraine,” the chairperson of the Standing Committee on Labor and Social Affairs said.
Belarus has consistently adhered to a peace-loving position, providing safe humanitarian channels, corridors, and places for organizing exchanges between Russia and Ukraine. More than 70 such events have already been held in Belarus.
                    
                    
                                        
                                    
                                                        
                
                
            Belarus continues to fulfill its humanitarian mission and once again served as a place for the prisoner exchange. Russia and Ukraine swapped over 103 people each.
The Belarusian side arranged the necessary logistical chain creating the conditions for the safe landing of the aircraft at Gomel airport and for the movement of a convoy of buses to the Novaya Guta border checkpoint where the exchange took place.
Each person was provided with hot meals. Adding a touch of tradition, the dry rations included apples and honey, the symbolic offerings of the Orthodox Savior's Feast which is marked on 19 August.For people who had spent a long time away from their families and loved ones and had experienced stressful situations, faith became a true salvation.
Ambulance teams were on hand, ready to provide medical assistance.
Natalya Masterskaya, Deputy Head of the Main Healthcare Directorate of the Gomel Oblast Executive Committee, emphasized that the presence of medical personnel is a necessity during such exchange operations. There were more than 70 of them. Over nearly 2.5 years, medical assistance has been provided to more than 1,500 prisoners of war from both sides. “For us, this is a great responsibility because prisoners of war arrive with various health conditions ranging from satisfactory to extremely severe. We provide each person with the necessary medical care in full right on the spot, and if necessary, we hospitalize them in healthcare institutions of the region. If surgical intervention is required, we perform it or transfer the patient to a higher-level facility, to national healthcare institutions in Minsk,” she said.
Medical assistance is provided equally to prisoners of war from both Russia and Ukraine. Most of the patients have sustained injuries. “Therefore, we perform primary surgical debridement, carry out surgical interventions, and treat complications since these are typically severe patients. We also receive people with strokes; they are hospitalized in intensive care units and undergo rehabilitation treatment. We provide the full spectrum and the entire range of necessary medical care,” Natalya Masterskaya said.
Each ambulance crew is equipped with everything necessary. “We already have experience and are aware of what to expect. So each team carries the necessary stock of medical supplies and medications. Of course, we have a supply of bandages, painkillers, and antiemetics and also blood pressure-lowering medications, antipyretics, and others. We have all the necessary drugs,” Natalya Masterskaya assured.
The main desire of every prisoner of war is to return home as soon as possible and hug their loved ones. One of the Ukrainian servicemen, Igor, tries to keep his spirits up: “My wife, children, mother, and father are waiting for me at home. I’m going back happy. I'm alive."
Two years and eight months of waiting for the exchange were also a serious test for Taras. “I can’t wait to get home. Finally, I'll see my loved ones - my mother, children, wife. We managed to correspond. A letter came from my mother. Everyone is waiting for me,” he said, his voice trembling.

Bilateral ties in focus as Syria's top diplomat makes trip to Pakistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:40:00 UTC
18:40:00 KST

Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani was set to arrive in Islamabad Wednesday evening for a two-day visit to Pakistan, a Pakistani Foreign Ministry source said.
Al-Shaibani will be in Pakistan on Aug. 19-20 at the invitation of his counterpart, Ishaq Dar, said the source, who asked not to be named.
The trip will mark the highest-level visit by a Syrian official to Pakistan since the overthrow of Bashar Assad in 2024, although other Syrian ministers have visited Islamabad since then.
It will also be the first visit by a Syrian foreign minister to Pakistan in 19 years.
In addition to talks with Dar, al-Shaibani is expected to meet Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and other ministers.
The last Syrian foreign minister to visit Pakistan was Walid al-Mouallem, who traveled to Islamabad in May 2007.
A Pakistani delegation met al-Shaibani in Damascus in June last year.
In March, the Pakistani prime minister discussed the ongoing escalation in the Middle East with Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa during a telephone call.
Al-Shaibani was appointed foreign minister under President al-Sharaa's administration following the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024.
His visit comes as Islamabad on Wednesday "strongly" condemned Israel's unprovoked attack on the Abu al-Duhur Airbase in Syria's northwestern Idlib province.
The two sides are expected to discuss ways to revive and expand cooperation in various fields, including the economy and defense, according to the source.
Islamabad and Damascus have maintained decadeslong relations, strengthened by military cooperation and training exchanges.
Pakistan's Embassy in Damascus remained open following Assad's overthrow, although bilateral cooperation between the two countries has remained limited over the past two years.
Pakistan and Syria formally established diplomatic relations in December 1949, two years after the creation of Pakistan.
Bilateral trade between Pakistan and Syria remains modest, totaling just $8.49 million.

Albania protests escalate as fight over land and power deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:39:56 UTC
18:39:56 KST

Breadcrumb
'What happens in Palestine does not stay in Palestine': Albania's Flamingo Revolution and the fight over land, power and sovereignty
Since mid-May 2026, protesters have gathered every day in cities across Albania, making the mobilisation one of the longest-running continuous protest movements in recent years.
The protests began as opposition to a luxury tourism development on the uninhabited island of Sazan, while developing into a national and transnational campaign challenging the Albanian government's model of development, the privatisation and exploitation of the land, and the country's increasingly political alignment with Western and Israeli interests.
The demonstrations, now widely known as the Flamingo Revolution, have brought together an unusually broad coalition of environmental activists, students, artists, architects, trade unionists and civil society groups.
Among the movement's most interesting voices is Fioralba Duma, an activist with Palestina e Lirë (Free Palestine in Albanian), who has participated in the protests since day one.
Over the past two years, Fioralba became the most important activist against Prime Minister Edi Rama's migration agreement with Italy, the externalisation of European borders through migrant detention centres in Albania, and what she describes as the growing convergence between environmental dispossession, colonial politics and solidarity with Palestine.
Speaking to The New Arab, Fioralba argues that the protests are no longer simply about Sazan, but have become a broader struggle over who owns Albania's land, who benefits from its development, and how global political conflicts increasingly shape domestic politics.
The origins of the movement
While the movement exploded onto the international scene over three months ago, opposition to the project dates back several years.
Activists say concerns first emerged around 2021, when plans for large-scale tourism projects began to surface for Sazan Island and other protected coastal areas.
For Fioralba Duma, the controversy reflects a much longer process.
"People had been talking about it since at least last year, I'd actually say since around 2021, when we first started noticing development initiatives that would later become connected to the project. We all knew the island was going to be handed over to private investors," she tells The New Arab.
"Today, the island is uninhabited, although during the communist period it had a school, a cinema, and other public facilities. It is, however, a strategically important island, both geographically and environmentally."
The controversy intensified after the Albanian parliament approved legislation allowing the construction of tourism infrastructure, including resorts, in certain categories of protected areas.
The decision came shortly after Albania and Italy ratified the migration agreement, prompting demonstrations against both measures.
The turning point, however, came after private security guards assaulted protesters near the fenced-off construction site in Zvërnec. Videos of the violence quickly spread across Albanian social media, transforming it into a national political issue.
"The footage provoked widespread indignation," Fioralba recalls. "The following day, we organised a demonstration in Tirana."
As the demonstrations continued, the focus quickly expanded beyond Sazan itself. According to Fioralba, the movement has become a broader challenge to Albania's development model, raising questions about who controls the country's natural resources and the country itself.
"At the heart of the mobilisation is a broader debate over ownership and the public interest. It is not simply about private versus public property, but about protecting places that belong to society as a whole rather than to oligarchic interests," she says.
Protesters have also focused on Law No. 21 of 2024, which allows new tourism developments in certain protected areas.
Activists argue that the legislation, together with the dismantling of protections for several protected areas, reflects a wider shift in Albania's approach to environmental governance.
Fioralba pointed to the Vjosa River, where, although the river itself remains protected, parts of its surrounding ecosystem lie outside the protected area.
She also situates these facts within the "Albania One Euro" model. The initiative was launched in 2006 under former Prime Minister Sali Berisha to encourage investment through favourable concession terms.
During the protests, activists also turned to The Albanian Files: Freedom and Architecture, an almost 800-page publication documenting hundreds of architectural and urban development projects across the country.
Copies of the book were scanned, shared and discussed during demonstrations as protesters sought to map connections between political power and what is happening on their land.
A struggle over Albania's future
The movement has also placed renewed scrutiny on corruption, money laundering and the role of foreign capital in reshaping Albania's landscape.
Fioralba argues that major developments increasingly benefit international investors while sidelining local communities and Albanian architects, who, she says, are routinely excluded from the projects.
For many protesters, this has also shaped the meaning of patriotism: defending forests, rivers and coastlines has become inseparable from defending Albania itself against economic dispossession and the enclosure of the commons.
"The fence represented the physical and symbolic enclosure of a place that people felt belonged to everyone," she explains. "It made visible the broader struggle over who has the right to the country's land and future."
One of the most widely shared images was an AI-generated illustration depicting a fictional border between Albania and Israel — a deliberately provocative piece that linked Jared Kushner's investment projects to wider debates about settler colonialism, land dispossession and Israel's ongoing genocide in Gaza.
"Although the protest did not initially receive widespread public support, the reaction to that image and to the demonstrations showed that Palestine, colonialism and the role of Israel already resonated deeply with many people," Fioralba adds.
As demonstrations continued day after day, the movement rapidly spread throughout the country, while solidarity actions were organised by Albanian diaspora communities in Italy, elsewhere in Europe, the United States and Australia.
At its peak, organisers estimate that around 100,000 people participated — a remarkable mobilisation in a country of roughly 2.3 million inhabitants.
One of the defining characteristics of the Flamingo Revolution has been its ability to unite movements that had long operated separately.
Environmental campaigners, artists, architects, students, designers and long-time political activists have found themselves marching together, transforming what began as an environmental campaign into one of the broadest social coalitions Albania has seen in years.
For Fioralba, that convergence did not happen by chance. "If you look around the protests today, you see environmental activists, designers, artists, students — people who have spent years working on very different causes," she says.
"A friend once joked that it feels as though all of us spent years participating in small, isolated protests simply to prepare for something like this. In a way, that's exactly how it feels."
Rather than creating a new movement from scratch, the protests became a meeting point for struggles that had been developing independently.
Environmental justice, anti-corruption campaigns, artistic activism and grassroots organising suddenly found a common political language through the defence of Sazan and Albanian land.
"We were building experiences, relationships and political awareness separately, until a moment arrived when all of those struggles suddenly converged," Fioralba continues.
"That is why this movement is different. It is not only about one project or one environmental campaign. It has become a space where many different political and social struggles have found a common language."
Fioralba also believes the unprecedented global mobilisations for Palestine helped reshape Albania's protest culture.
While she acknowledges that Albania has experienced major demonstrations before — notably the student movement — she argues that Palestine contributed something different: it normalised public protest for a new generation and offered a political framework through which many people interpreted the developments unfolding in their own country.
"Palestine acted like a kind of fuel. It helped people overcome a certain attachment to the dominant narrative of 'development.' It offered a different lens through which to understand what was happening in Albania," she says.
Palestine in the Albanian Revolution
If the movement has challenged Albania's development model, Fioralba believes it has also begun to reshape how many Albanians imagine the country's future.
One of its most significant achievements, she argues, has been opening a public conversation that would have been almost unthinkable only a few years ago.
Albania's post-communist history, she says, produced an almost unquestionable attachment to private property. After nearly five decades of state socialism, ownership became synonymous with freedom, making criticism of privatisation or large-scale investment politically difficult.
"There are still people who take the microphone during demonstrations and feel the need to clarify: 'We are not against private investors. We are not against wealthy people. We are against those who destroy the environment, who operate without transparency, and who act with impunity.'"
Yet Fioralba believes the Flamingo Revolution has begun to erode those assumptions.
Many protesters have begun questioning an economic model centred on speculative investment, environmental destruction, and the privatisation of public goods, while demanding stronger public education, healthcare, and social protections.
"I would never have expected this from a society that experienced one of Europe's harshest communist dictatorships. Yet this is exactly what I have witnessed. After 35 years of what we call 'turbo-capitalism,' more and more Albanians are beginning to imagine a different future," she says.
For Fioralba, that political transformation also explains why Palestina e Lirë became deeply involved in these struggles. Although the collective was founded in solidarity with Gaza, its members soon concluded that the mechanisms they opposed in Palestine could also be recognised elsewhere.
"We quickly realised that what happens in Palestine does not stay in Palestine," Fioralba adds.
According to the activist, a series of political developments reinforced that conviction: the expansion of Albania's defence industry following Antony Blinken's 2024 visit, the Rama-Meloni migration agreement, the deepening strategic relationship between Tirana and Rome, Prime Minister Edi Rama's growing engagement with Israeli political leaders, and what activists perceive as an increasing alignment of Albania with broader Western geopolitical interests.
Taken individually, she says, each event might appear unrelated. Viewed together, however, they reveal what the movement considers a broader political trajectory.
The result has been a growing debate over what Palestina e Lirë calls Albania's "complicity."
Rather than treating Palestine as a distant foreign policy issue, the collective argues that the same political and economic relationships destroying Gaza also influence decisions about land inside Albania.
"People kept asking us: 'Why do you care so much about Palestine? Why don't you care about Albania?' For us, that has always been a false distinction," she explains.
Fioralba argues that Albania's own history — marked by foreign intervention, the partition of Albanian-inhabited territories by the European Powers, and collective memories of genocide and displacement — has fostered the idea that promises of external investment are crucial to the country's stability.
Yet she believes projects proposed for Sazan, Zvërnec, and Lake Butrint changed this perception.
"We see them as different expressions of what we describe as the 'Israelisation' of Albania — a model in which territory, strategic assets and public resources are increasingly subordinated to external political and economic interests," Fioralba concludes.
Dalia Ismail is a Palestinian-Italian independent analyst and journalist

Nuclear material found at site will remain in Syria: Syrian FM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:38:59 UTC
18:38:59 KST

Breadcrumb
Nuclear material found at site will remain in Syria, right to civilian use: Syrian FM
Nuclear material discovered at an undisclosed site in Syria is not dangerous and will remain in Syrian custody, subject to guarantees from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said on Tuesday.
During a joint press conference in Damascus with IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi, the foreign minister added that Syria had the right to use this material for civil and peaceful purposes.
"On July 17, we sent an official letter to the agency, in which we voluntarily declared the presence of nuclear materials at an undeclared site, part of the legacy left by the old regime", Shaibani said.
"According to technical assessments, these materials present no risk", assured the Syrian minister. "These matters will remain in Syria's custody, while being subject to the agency's supervision system", he said.
The head of the UN's nuclear watchdog said on Tuesday its inspectors had found several tons of nuclear material in Syria, at a site Damascus reported to the agency last month.
The inspectors visited two sites, one in Deir Ezzor and "a second location related to the nuclear material identified by Syria recently", according to a joint statement.
Speaking at a news conference in Damascus, Rafael Grossi, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), praised Damascus's "courageous decision" to report the undisclosed site, which dates back to the rule of ousted former dictator Bashar-al-Assad.
"We are talking about a few tons of nuclear material that could be put to bad use," he said, promising that it would be put under international safeguards.
Grossi said "this material will be accounted for, will be put within the international safeguards system".
Syrian and IAEA experts will work together to safely store the materials, he said.
"We are starting to turn a page, and turning a page does not mean forgetting the past," he added.
Likely from reactor
Grossi also visited a site in Deir al-Zour in the east, which has been shut for 18 years after an Israeli attack on the site.
In 2008, less than a year after the strike, US officials accused Syria of having sought to build a secret nuclear reactor and acknowledged that Israel had destroyed it in the raid.
The UN atomic watchdog declared in 2011 that the Syrian site was "very likely" to have been a nuclear reactor, adding that information provided to it suggested that it was being built with North Korean assistance.
Pierre Razoux, academic director of French think tank the FMES Institute, told AFP the nuclear materials found on Tuesday are "most likely... linked to the Syrian nuclear program, which was halted in 2007 after the Israeli raid on the Al-Kibar site" in Deir al-Zour.
He said, however, that Syria may also have nuclear materials that Iraq rid itself of at the start of the 2000s.
Grossi said the find vindicated the IAEA's longstanding suspicion that Syria had been secretly building a reactor and that the agency was "at the... site of Deir al-Zour, where a very comprehensive work of excavation and exploration is taking place now".
The watchdog said last year that it had discovered uranium particles at the site during an inspection in 2024.
Grossi's visit came after news outlet Axios last week quoted US and Israeli officials as saying Washington and the IAEA reached an agreement to have the watchdog remove nuclear material stored at a clandestine site in Syria after having "reached understandings with Syria and Israel".
Axios said Israel, a nuclear-armed state, was closely monitoring a location called "Site 99", where Israeli officials say the Assad government stored nuclear material that was part of the Deir al-Zour project, also known as "Al-Kibar", and that Israel had threatened to bomb it.

Russia and Ukraine exchange 103 POWs – MOD (VIDEO)

The soldiers will later be transported to Russia for further treatment and rehabilitation at Defense Ministry medical facilities.
During the exchange, Lantratova met Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmitry Lubinets. The two sides exchanged lists of missing persons, as well as letters from relatives for servicemen who remain in captivity. They also agreed to arrange the delivery of parcels to POWs held by both sides.
The exchange was carried out with humanitarian mediation from the United Arab Emirates, the ministry added.
The swap is the latest in a series of prisoner exchanges between Moscow and Kiev despite the ongoing conflict.
The previous exchange took place on June 26, when the two sides returned 160 servicemen each, also with UAE mediation. Earlier that month, Russia and Ukraine also exchanged 185 POWs each, while another 205 servicemen from each side were released in May.
Moscow and Kiev have also continued exchanging the bodies of fallen soldiers. The UAE has repeatedly acted as a mediator in humanitarian contacts between the two sides.

What happened to the Nord Stream pipelines?
The Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines were set up to deliver Russian gas to Germany and other countries in Europe.
Nord Stream 2 had yet to enter service when in September 2022, both pipelines were damaged by blasts that rendered them inoperable.
The blasts came just months after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Germany has said it believes the blasts were sabotage ordered by unspecified Ukrainian state entities but Kyiv has so far denied involvement.
Prosecutors have said the plot aimed to permanently disrupt gas deliveries via the pipelines and prevent Moscow from using the revenue generated from natural gas trading to finance its military operations.
Moscow had repeatedly reduced or suspended deliveries through Nord Stream 1 after starting the invasion, blaming Western sanctions and technical issues.
Europe, in its turn, accused Russia of weaponizing energy supplies.

NASA releases first IMAGES of SpaceX lunar crash crater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:36:02 UTC
18:36:02 KST

NASA releases first IMAGES of SpaceX lunar crash crater
NASA has released images showing a crater blasted into the Moon by a discarded SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket stage that struck the lunar surface at around 5,400 mph (8,700 kph) earlier this month.
The US space agency published an animated before-and-after comparison on Tuesday, using images captured by its Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) that show the previously undisturbed surface and a dark new impact scar.
NASA said the crater measures roughly 18 meters (60 ft) across and less than 3 meters (10 ft) deep.
The images also reveal bright and dark rays spreading outward from the crater. NASA said the darker streaks consist of weathered lunar dust and rocks that were blasted out from the upper 1.5 ft (0.46 m) of the lunar surface by the impact. The material had been altered over time by solar wind, cosmic rays, and micrometeorite strikes. Brighter debris near the crater rim came from deeper underground.
Spotted: Falcon 9 impact site 
NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) has captured images of a new crater on the Moon. The crater formed on Aug. 5, 2026, when a SpaceX Falcon 9 upper stage impacted the lunar surface. https://t.co/aqduBYwpmgpic.twitter.com/hE83yvzmIk
The 4-ton upper stage struck the Moon on August 5 after drifting through space for more than a year. The Falcon 9 launched in January 2025 carrying the US Blue Ghost and Japanese Resilience lunar landers. Its reusable first-stage booster returned to Earth, while the second stage remained in space.
SpaceX said the stage had initially been placed on a trajectory considered safe under existing rules. A combination of solar activity and gravitational forces later sent it toward the lunar surface.
Although the Moon is regularly struck by natural meteoroids, collisions involving man-made objects are much less common. NASA deliberately crashed rocket stages into the lunar surface during the Apollo era to collect seismic data.
Experts have warned that unplanned impacts could become a greater concern as human activity on and around the Moon increases. UK aerospace engineer Dean Sladen told Space.com last week that uncontrolled rocket stages could become a “tangible operational risk” as space agencies and private companies build permanent lunar infrastructure.

UAE suspends trade, financial transactions with Iran after attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:36:01 UTC
18:36:01 KST

The United Arab Emirates has suspended "all trade, commercial exchange and financial transactions with Iran" after the Islamic Republic attacked a number of UAE-owned tankers and rejected new talks with the US, the UAE’s foreign ministry announced late on Monday night.
Only shortly before UAE Ministry of Foreign Affairs Director of Strategic Communications Afra Al Hameli made the statement, Iran fired two missiles toward the emirates, one of which fell within their territorial waters, while the second landed outside its territory.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei on Tuesday denied that Iran was behind the launches, claiming, according to state media, that the “allegation runs counter to the principle of good-neighborliness and undermines ongoing efforts to strengthen trust among regional countries and prevent a further escalation of insecurity in the region.”
Despite Baqaei’s comment, the Islamic Republic has launched numerous attacks on countries across the Middle East since February 28, when the US and Israel attacked the Islamic regime. According to The National news site, at least a dozen people have been killed in the UAE during the conflict and over 200 wounded.
"The United Arab Emirates rejects all claims regarding the status of its economic relations with the Islamic Republic of Iran, while reaffirming its steadfast commitment to dialogue, co-operation and regional integration as essential means to enhance peace, stability, and prosperity in the region," Hameli said in a statement on X/Twitter.
Financial relations in the Gulf appear to be rapidly changing.
Saudi Arabia has placed financial transfers to the UAE under extra layers of regulatory oversight reserved for countries considered high-risk for illicit money flows, according to Reuters, citing three individuals with knowledge of the matter.
The measures, which were not announced publicly, could help explain why a number of companies say they have had difficulties transferring funds from accounts in Saudi Arabia to the UAE in recent months, an issue first reported by Bloomberg and the Financial Times in July. The enhanced oversight measures have not previously been reported.
Commenting on this reported development, UAE-based analyst Kristian Alexander told The Jerusalem Post that he would be “somewhat cautious” in interpreting Riyadh’s additional scrutiny of financial transfers “as evidence of a broader Saudi effort directed against the UAE.”
“There is an important regulatory dimension here. Saudi Arabia, like the UAE, has considerably strengthened its anti-money-laundering, counter-terrorist-financing and financial compliance frameworks in recent years,” he said. “In a period of heightened regional uncertainty, additional due diligence on particular categories of cross-border transactions can therefore have legitimate regulatory and risk-management explanations.”
Though reluctant to entirely attribute the development to a souring of relations, Alexander acknowledged that the report came as Riyadh and Abu Dhabi evolved. Remaining “exceptionally important economic and security partners,” Alexander said that the two states did not “necessarily have identical interests or policy preferences on every regional and economic issue,” including on issues relating to the governance of Yemen and regional conflicts.
Both countries are also pursuing ambitious national development strategies that naturally create a degree of competition in areas such as investment, logistics, tourism, aviation, financial services, and the attraction of multinational companies,” he said.
“I would therefore describe the relationship less in terms of a ‘rift’ and more as a maturing relationship in which close cooperation increasingly coexists with economic competition and occasional policy differences. That is not particularly unusual between two states whose economies and regional ambitions have expanded considerably over the past decade.”
Alexander said the more critical issue was whether a period of somewhat greater policy differentiation “could slow the momentum toward deeper GCC economic integration.”
Should regulatory frameworks, investment policies, and national economic strategies increasingly diverge, businesses may have to adapt to two increasingly distinct economic environments, he warned, adding that such a development would not constitute a political crisis, but it would disrupt efforts to create a more integrated Gulf economic space.
Though the major financial changes in the Gulf have seemed to come into place within a short period of time, Alexander said he would again be cautious about drawing a direct causal connection between the two developments.
“The chronology is important. According to Reuters, enhanced Saudi scrutiny of certain UAE-bound financial transfers appears to have been introduced earlier in 2026, while the UAE's decision to suspend trade, commercial exchanges and financial transactions with Iran came considerably later, following the latest deterioration in the regional security environment,” he continued.
“On the evidence currently available, therefore, I do not think we can conclude that the Saudi measures were introduced specifically in response to UAE-Iran commercial relations,” he added.
Despite this, Alexander said the indirect relationship between the two states’ financial decisions might lie in the fact that both developments have occurred as the region is facing a greater sense of uncertainty in consequence of Iranian attacks and where governments are paying greater attention to financial exposure, trade flows, maritime security, and the potential economic consequences of regional conflict.
“I would therefore view the Saudi and Emirati measures as primarily separate decisions arising from different immediate circumstances but taking place within the same increasingly complex regional security environment. It would be premature to establish a direct connection between them without additional evidence,” Alexander said.

Taipei Zoo continues critical care for premature orangutan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:31:37 UTC
18:31:37 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei Zoo on Wednesday shared an update on Da Pao, a premature Bornean orangutan receiving intensive medical care, saying the infant continues to gain weight and shows signs of improvement but remains in critical care.
The update came on International Orangutan Day, as the zoo provided information about the twin orangutans born by cesarean section to mother Ke Yi at the end of June. The other twin, Hsiao Pao, died shortly after birth from respiratory distress syndrome, per a zoo press release.
The zoo said Da Pao was born with its lungs and other organs not yet fully developed. The infant required an endotracheal tube and ventilator to assist with breathing. Its ability to breathe independently has gradually improved, allowing medical staff to remove the endotracheal tube.
However, because Da Pao previously experienced lung collapse and inflammation, it continues to require oxygen support through a high-flow nasal cannula, the zoo said. The infant's digestive system is also not fully developed, and it has experienced bloating and other digestive problems.
Its overall physiological condition requires round-the-clock monitoring. A cross-disciplinary medical team, including support from the Neonatal Department at National Taiwan University Hospital, has been invaluable.
The zoo said Da Pao's weight has been steadily increasing. Activity level, including limb movements and responses to external stimuli, has also improved. Zoo staff have recently begun bottle-feeding to help it practice sucking and swallowing, per the press release.
The zoo also highlighted the conservation challenges facing Bornean orangutans, which are classified as critically endangered. Wild populations face threats including deforestation, habitat fragmentation, human-wildlife conflict, illegal hunting, and the wildlife trade.
Orangutans reproduce slowly, with females typically giving birth every six to eight years. Young orangutans depend on their mothers for an extended period to learn essential survival skills, including foraging and nest building. As a result, the zoo said, once orangutan populations decline, recovery can take considerable time.

Taiwan legislative speaker clashes with premier over refusal to countersign laws
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:31:17 UTC
18:31:17 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Legislative Yuan Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) clashed with Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) on Tuesday after Cho announced Monday that he would refuse to countersign two more bills passed by the legislature.
Han cautioned the Cabinet against refusing to countersign the Act Governing Savings Accounts for Future Education and Development of Children and Youth and amendments to the Cable Radio and Television Act, per Tai Sounds. He warned that if the Cabinet believes it can refuse to enforce or countersign legislation passed by the legislature, Taiwan’s constitutional order would be put in peril.
Han questioned the Cabinet’s legal authority to use the premier’s countersigning power as a veto over passed legislation. He stressed that the executive branch should not treat the Cabinet as the Constitutional Court, which serves as a mechanism for resolving disputes between Taiwan’s branches of government.
Cho responded by citing Article 37 of the Constitution, which states that laws promulgated or orders issued by the president require the premier’s countersignature, per Liberty Times. He argued that he has the authority to refuse to countersign legislation passed by the legislature.
Cho also cited Article 91 of the Budget Act and Article 70 of the Constitution, arguing that the legislature has no authority to pass legislation that would increase the executive branch’s fiscal burden, per UDN. He said the executive branch was forced to respond to what he described as “the legislature’s repeated attacks against Taiwan’s constitutional order under Han.”
Cho said he hoped to resolve the imbalance in the constitutional system. Sources close to Han suggested that after Han publicly criticized KMT Caucus Convener Fu Kun-chi (傅崐萁) to help push through the 2026 budget, the government’s refusal to countersign two more bills prompted his Facebook criticism, per UDN.
DPP Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) echoed Cho’s argument, saying the Constitution authorizes the premier to refuse to countersign legislation, per NOWNews. He said that while the executive branch is not above the Constitution, a legislative majority cannot violate the supreme law at will.
Kaohsiung Mayor Chen Chi-mai (陳其邁) suggested that the root of the dispute was the opposition’s boycott of Constitutional Court nominees, per CNA. While the Constitutional Court was briefly paralyzed by a lack of new nominees, it has since resumed operations following a controversial ruling.
TPP Legislative Caucus Convener Chen Ching-lung (陳清龍) criticized Cho’s use of the countersigning power, noting that under the Constitution, the Cabinet should request reconsideration of legislation it believes would be difficult to enforce, per Z.Media. KMT Legislator Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) argued that Lai should have intervened to resolve the legislative deadlock rather than allowing the conflict between the executive and legislative branches to worsen, per Tai Sounds.
On whether Cho has the authority to refuse to countersign legislation passed by the legislature, pro-DPP legal commentator and lawyer Huang Ti-ying (黃帝穎) argued that the opposition’s refusal to initiate a vote of no confidence legitimizes Cho’s decision, per SETN. If a vote of no confidence succeeds, Lai may dissolve the legislature and trigger a new legislative election.
Soochow University Professor Su Tzu-chiao (蘇子喬) said the countersigning mechanism was designed to check presidential power in a semi-presidential system, per UDN. However, former President Lee Teng-hui (李登輝) consolidated the power to appoint premiers under the sole discretion of the president, rendering the mechanism largely moot.
Su said the Cabinet should ask the legislature to reconsider bills it believes may be difficult to enforce. He stressed that the repeated use of the refusal to countersign, which was first used when the Constitutional Court was paralyzed, is a major concern now that the court is functioning again.
Su recommended that the Cabinet seek recourse through the Constitutional Court, adding that the legislature should also consider asking the court to intervene over the use of the countersigning power.
Retired Tunghai University Professor Lin Teng-yau (林騰鷂) noted that the constitutional provision concerning countersigning appears in the chapter governing presidential powers, per ETtoday. He said requirements such as countersigning or legislative authorization for certain presidential powers were designed as safeguards against potential presidential abuse of power.
Lin warned that before the Constitutional Court rules a law unconstitutional, the Cabinet does not have the authority to unilaterally declare it unconstitutional. He cautioned that reinterpreting a constitutional mechanism could become a means of expanding executive power.

US removes Nigeria from decade-long port security restrictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:29:05 UTC
18:29:05 KST

US removes Nigeria from decade-long port security restrictions
The US has lifted security restrictions on vessels arriving from Nigeria, ending a 12-year regime that burdened shipping companies with additional guards, inspections, and paperwork.
A US Coast Guard notice published on Wednesday said “recent assessments” had found that Africa’s most populous nation was maintaining effective antiterrorism measures at its ports, warranting the removal of restrictions known as Conditions of Entry (CoE).
The measures, imposed in June 2014, did not amount to an outright ban on Nigerian-flagged ships. They applied to vessels that had called at designated Nigerian ports during their previous five port calls, requiring operators to tighten onboard security, guard access points, and report their precautions. The safeguards were intended to prevent ships leaving poorly secured ports from being exploited to carry terrorists, weapons, or tampered cargo into US waters.
The conditions had long drawn complaints over higher insurance bills, added personnel costs, and delays. Abuja expects their removal to improve turnaround times and attract shipping lines, although congestion, corruption allegations, and Gulf of Guinea piracy remain obstacles.
The Nigerian Maritime Administration and Safety Agency said the US Coast Guard conducted four assessments of the West African nation’s maritime security systems and port facilities between March 2024 and April 2026.
The agency said in a statement on Tuesday that it expects the lifting of the CoE “to improve port competitiveness, enhance vessel turnaround and schedule reliability, reduce additional security-related costs and strengthen Nigeria’s position in global shipping.”
Nigeria’s minister of marine and blue economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, hailed the decision as “a major milestone” affirming Abuja’s progress in maritime security and implementation of the International Ship and Port Facility Security Code.
“We will sustain this momentum and ensure Nigeria remains a safe, secure and competitive destination for international shipping,” he wrote on X.
Nigeria was not the only African country subject to US conditions of entry. Similar vessel restrictions remain in force against Cameroon, Comoros, Equatorial Guinea, The Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Libya, Madagascar, Seychelles, Sudan, and Sao Tome and Principe. In February, the Coast Guard expanded the restrictions within Cameroon and Madagascar by revoking exemptions previously granted to certain port facilities.

French Couple Seeks Body of Russia-Born Son Killed Fighting for Ukraine
A French couple is fighting to recover the body of their adopted son, killed by Russian artillery in Ukraine's Zaporizhzhia region on April 14, 2025, from a battlefield they cannot safely reach.
The story of Alexis Lenouail and his parents, Jean-Philippe and Nathalie, of France's Morbihan department, was reported by the French regional newspaper La Montagne on August 17.
He was 23 when he was killed during his first combat mission alongside his unit.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The couple learned of their son's death not from a phone call or an officer at their door, but from social media. A photograph and a short French message—"Homage to our brothers"—appeared on the Instagram profile of an International Legion soldier.
Alexis had gone a week without contact after warning that he was leaving on a mission with his unit. Russian artillery cut him down on April 14, 2025, in the Zaporizhzhia region, killing several of his comrades in the same barrage, the newspaper wrote.
Alexis, whose callsign was “Hector,“ had been adopted from a Russian orphanage in Murom, about 200 kilometers east of Moscow, in the autumn of 2003, when he was ten months old.
Born in Russia, he would be killed two decades later fighting its army in Ukraine.
His parents described an energetic boy who dreamed of becoming a knight and of protecting the people he loved. After earning a BTS diploma in international commerce at Saint-Malo, he announced his wish to enlist.
In January 2021, he began training for the entrance tests of France's 93rd Mountain Artillery Regiment at Varces, in Isère. He passed, but grew restless whenever the action stopped, and eventually told his father, "Dad, I'm going to Ukraine."
More than a year on, the family is caught between two ordeals: grieving a son whose body lies beyond reach, and a French administrative process slow to formally recognize him as killed in combat.
"We know where he is, but we can't go and get him," the couple stated, describing remains in an active combat zone where any recovery depends first on security and access to the ground.
Under the Geneva Conventions, warring parties are required to take all possible measures to search for, collect, and identify the dead and to inform their families, though that duty does not guarantee retrieval from a contested battlefield. The International Committee of the Red Cross reported in February 2026 that its tracing bureau was working to clarify the fate of nearly 217,000 people connected to the war. The figure is a caseload, not a definitive total of the missing.
The way Alexis's parents learned of his death, through an online post rather than an official notification, echoes what other foreign volunteers' families have faced.
An Italian volunteer, 42-year-old Alex Pineschi, was killed in May 2026 while serving in a Ukrainian military intelligence unit. News of his death surfaced first in online communities of foreign fighters, and he was counted as the 11th Italian citizen to die in the war. By 2025, Ukraine's forces had drawn volunteers from more than 70 countries.
In July 2026, Ukraine recovered the bodies of 501 people that Russia identified as Ukrainian service members, part of a series of exchanges that have grown more frequent since peace talks resumed in early 2025.

The party lost 0.2 percentage points from the previous HS poll in July. Its support has not fallen below the latest figure in the newspaper’s polling since 2021.
The opposition Social Democratic Party remains Finland’s most popular party with 23.8 per cent support. Its rating was unchanged from July, leaving it 7.3 percentage points ahead of National Coalition.
The Finns Party, which sits in Orpo’s government, rose 0.4 percentage points to 14.6 per cent and moved ahead of the opposition Centre Party, which remained at 13.7 per cent.
The Finns Party has recorded the largest increase over the past year among the parties. Its support has risen from 11 per cent in August 2025 to 14.6 per cent.
Combined support for the four government parties stands at 38.1 per cent, according to the HS poll.
The Left Alliance received 11.3 per cent, down 0.2 percentage points from July, while the Greens remained at 8.8 per cent. Movement Now recorded 2.3 per cent. The Swedish People’s Party and Christian Democrats recorded no major changes.
Most month-on-month movements remained within the poll’s margin of error.
Research company Verian conducted the survey for Helsingin Sanomat between 14 July and 17 August. It interviewed 2,946 people through an online panel.
The polling period included political debate over the Garden Helsinki project. Parliament interrupted its summer recess in July to discuss the project and Orpo’s links to the plans.
The survey also coincided with debate over funding for social and healthcare organisations and the Ceuta border crisis.
The margin of error for the largest parties is about 1.8 percentage points in either direction.

Seoul to introduce citywide shades as extreme heat waves swelter South Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-19
09:24:39 UTC
18:24:39 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
19 August 2026•Update: 19 August 2026
The local government in South Korea's capital Seoul on Wednesday announced a new urban initiative to establish "right to shade" as a fundamental municipal policy, according to daily The Korea Times.
The plan aims to guarantee continuous, shaded pedestrian routes across the capital, treating access to cooling as an essential public service rather than a geographical privilege.
Following a pilot program next year across 10 areas, the city plans to roll out the initiative citywide beginning in 2028.
"Heat waves are no longer a temporary inconvenience that people can endure for a few days. As they grow more intense and last longer, they are becoming a routine disaster that threatens people’s lives and safety," Seoul Mayor Oh Se-hoon told a news conference.
Under the framework, the municipal government will link individual shaded spots, including broad-canopy trees, building shadows, retractable awnings, canopies, and gardens, into continuous walking corridors connecting residential neighborhoods with subway stations, schools, markets, and hospitals.
The initiative comes amid a sharp rise in heat-related casualties across South Korea. 
 
According to the Interior Ministry, 31 people had died from heat-related illnesses nationwide this year as of Monday, exceeding the 23 fatalities recorded throughout last year.
Additionally, 3,439 people have suffered from heat-related illnesses this year.
A municipal study of over 67,000 sidewalks across Seoul revealed that pedestrian routes were exposed to direct sunlight for an average of four hours and 21 minutes daily, with direct sun exposure exceeding six hours on nearly 28% of streets.
Data from the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency showed that streets and sidewalks were the most common setting for heat illness in Seoul, accounting for 31.4% of reported cases between 2023 and 2025.

Sources tell i24NEWS about disputes within the leadership of the Al-Qassam Brigades regarding the restriction of weapons, with one faction warning the move could be exploited to target the movement
Palestinian sources from within Hamas have revealed differences in positions and opinions among the leadership of the Qassam Brigades, the movement’s armed wing, regarding the political leadership’s decision to place weapons under centralized control as part of implementing the agreement reached between Hamas and the Board of Peace. Sources from within Hamas who spoke with i24NEWS say that the commander of the southern region, Mahmoud al-Barimm, who oversees the Khan Younis and Rafah brigades, considered, in a document he sent to the al-Qassam leadership and Hamas, that the process of inventorying weapons at this time would be unnecessary and would have major repercussions.

The sources noted that al-Barim was not the only one in taking this position, getting support from Commander of the Northern Brigade Izz al-Din al-Beik, whom Israel attempted to kill about two months ago in an attack targeting an apartment in which he was present alongside Imad Islim, the commander of the Zeitoun Battalion and deputy commander of the Gaza Brigade. Israel has often refused to reach an agreement with Hamas for a long-term truce that would freeze the use of weapons. It still insists on the complete disarmament of Hamas and the removal of its weapons from the Gaza Strip. Meanwhile, the Board of Peace has conveyed assurances to Israel that the weapons will be melted down and will not remain inside the Strip in any form, even though they will be restricted to the hands of a technocratic committee.
